caption: The Kleinmann-Low Nebula in the Orion Nebula complex, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Stars shining a vivid red are scattered through the clouds of this picture. They are the stars hidden inside the Kleinmann-Low Nebula, a part of the larger Orion Nebula complex, and they only show up because Hubble looked in near-infrared as well as optical light. The final mosaic was stitched together from several separate Hubble pointings.

Dust is the reason infrared matters. Star-forming clouds are thick with fine grains that block ordinary light, so in a visible-light picture many young stars stay buried. Longer infrared wavelengths slip through that dust much more easily, letting astronomers see the stars sitting inside the cloud.

The field covers the heart of the Orion Nebula, about 1,400 light-years away, and it was made with a specific hunt in mind. Researchers were searching for rogue planets, which drift without a parent star, and brown dwarfs, objects too small to shine as true stars. Along the way they found, by chance, a star racing through the region at high speed.
explore: The fast-moving star was a side result of the survey rather than its goal. Astronomers call such objects runaway stars, because they are travelling far faster than their neighbours in the nebula.
Combining optical and near-infrared observations lets one image show both the nebula and the stars its dust would otherwise hide.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 captured this scene in optical and near-infrared light. The exact colour assigned to each filter isn't published, though the caption notes the stars revealed by infrared appear bright red.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light that reveals the red stars is invisible to the human eye, so these stars would stay hidden behind dust to a viewer.

alt: A cloudy region of the Orion Nebula dotted with stars that glow bright red.

caption: The Exposed Cranium Nebula (PMR 1), imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A see-through bubble with a blue rim holds two off-white lobes, split down the middle by a dark lane. Seen whole, it looks like a brain inside a semi-transparent skull. This is the nebula PMR 1, nicknamed the Exposed Cranium, seen in mid-infrared light by Webb's MIRI instrument.

The shape records two separate chapters in the life of a dying star. First it threw off an outer shell made mostly of hydrogen. Later came a more tangled, structured mix of material, which now sits nearer the centre. The skull and the brain are those two episodes.

At the top, the dark lane ends in an oval where material seems to be erupting outwards, and MIRI shows this ejection more clearly than Webb's near-infrared camera does. A fainter twin may be pushing out of the bottom, which hints at a two-sided outflow. Further analysis could show what is driving it.
explore: In mid-infrared light more of the nebula's dust appears, while fewer stars and background galaxies show up than in Webb's NIRCam view. Comparing different infrared wavelengths should help astronomers judge how much material the central star is losing and what stage of its decline Webb has caught.

understand.summary: Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI) took this image through four mid-infrared filters, shown as blue (10 microns), green (11 microns), orange (12 microns) and red (18 microns).
understand.eye: Mid-infrared light is invisible to the human eye, so the colours here are a translation of light that we cannot see directly.

alt: A transparent bubble with a blue edge surrounding two off-white lobes separated by a dark vertical lane, resembling a brain seen from above, with a few faint galaxies around it.

caption: A sky field near the Chamaeleon I complex, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
captureDate: a few days before the Paranal Inauguration on 1 April 1999
story: This colour picture shows a patch of sky close to Chamaeleon I, a grouping of hot stars and bright nebulae in the southern constellation that shares its name. The region lies close to the southern celestial pole.

The image comes from the very start of the Very Large Telescope's working life. It was made with the FORS1 camera on ANTU, the first of the VLT's large unit telescopes, just days before the Paranal Observatory was inaugurated and formally handed over to astronomers.

Chamaeleon I is catalogued as a star-forming region, and its entry also lists dark nebula features, clouds of dust dense enough to block the light behind them. The picture itself is a quick look, built from six one-minute exposures taken through three different filters and combined into a single colour view.
explore: The field shown measures 6.8 by 11.2 arcminutes, with north at the top and east to the left. The region is about 500 light-years away.

understand.summary: The image was taken with the FORS1 instrument on the VLT's first unit telescope in visible and near-infrared light (V, R and I bands). How each band was coloured isn't published.
understand.eye: The camera combined several exposures, collecting far more faint light than the eye could gather from this part of the sky.

alt: A colour-composite view of a star field near the Chamaeleon I nebula complex.

caption: Cassiopeia A supernova remnant, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble view shows the tattered wreckage of a star that blew itself apart. The remnant is called Cassiopeia A, or Cas A for short, and it lies about 11,000 light-years away in the constellation Cassiopeia.

A supernova remnant is the expanding cloud of debris left behind when a massive star explodes. Cas A is the youngest known remnant of such an explosion in our own galaxy, the Milky Way. It is also catalogued as SN 1680.

Hubble's sharp eye picks out how complicated that debris is. Rather than forming a smooth, simple shell, the shattered fragments of the star make up a complex and intricate structure. The picture was made with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using three filters that record red and near-infrared light.
explore: The remnant is catalogued both as Cassiopeia A, named for the constellation in which it appears, and as SN 1680. The Hubble picture comes from the Advanced Camera for Surveys.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded this image through red and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the light used here is near-infrared, which the eye cannot see, and the long exposures reveal debris far too faint to see directly.

alt: The shattered, intricately structured remains of an exploded star.

caption: The reflection nebula NGC 2023 in Orion, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Soft sunset shades wash across this scene of billowing gas, with a few odd greenish clumps tucked into the waves. It is the southern part of NGC 2023, a reflection nebula in Orion lying nearly 1,500 light-years from Earth, not far from the Flame and Horsehead Nebulae.

The nebula glows because of a massive young B-type star, a hot, blue-white kind of star several times hotter than the Sun. Its light makes the nebula unusually bright. The star sits just out of view at the upper left, and the bright flare along the left side is its light scattered inside Hubble's optics, not part of the nebula.

Stars are still forming in NGC 2023. Astronomers think the greenish clumps are Herbig–Haro objects, patches where gas shot out of newborn stars at hundreds of kilometres per second slams into surrounding material and makes it glow. Such features usually fade within a few thousand years.
explore: The whole of NGC 2023 is about four light-years across, and its waves of gas are 5000 times denser than the interstellar medium. The field of view of this image is 3.2 arcminutes.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys took this image. A blue filter (F475W) is shown as blue, a yellow filter (F625W) as green, and a near-infrared filter (F850LP) as red.
understand.eye: The red channel records near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and total exposures of 800 to 1200 seconds per filter gather far more light than the eye could.

alt: Billowing waves of gas in sunset-like shades with unusual greenish clumps, and a bright flare along the left side.

caption: Sharpless 2-296 in the Seagull Nebula, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: Wispy, colourful clouds glow among dark lanes of dust and bright stars in this view. The glowing gas is Sharpless 2-296, which forms the outstretched wings of the Seagull Nebula, a region of sky named because it looks like a gull in flight.

The Seagull Nebula is a stellar nursery. It is made of dust, hydrogen and helium, with traces of heavier elements, and it is a hot, energetic birthplace of new stars. Clouds like this are called H II regions, because the intense light of young, hot stars strips electrons from the hydrogen gas around them and the gas glows in response.

The dark dust lanes are cooler, denser pockets of material that block the light behind them, and places like these are where future stars can form. The nebula lies about 3,500 light-years away in the constellation Monoceros.
explore: The image was captured by the OmegaCAM camera on the VLT Survey Telescope, as part of the VPHAS+ survey, using filters that include one tuned to the red glow of hydrogen.

understand.summary: The VLT Survey Telescope's OmegaCAM camera recorded this visible-light image through several broadband filters and a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The camera's long exposures build up faint glowing gas that the eye would struggle to see at all, even through a telescope.

alt: Colourful, wispy glowing clouds woven through dark dust lanes and bright stars.

caption: Part of the H II region N214 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by ESO's New Technology Telescope
story: A large nebula fills the lower part of this picture, a star cluster sits from the upper left to the middle, and a string of compact reddish nebulae lies at the top right. Together they are part of N214, a region of glowing gas in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy near our own.

Regions like this are called H II regions. Hot young stars pour out energetic light that strips hydrogen atoms of their electrons, and the gas glows as a result. The big nebula at the bottom is known as N214C.

The reddish knots at the upper right are N214H. The new observations show that it is made of four compact H II regions, each with its own star lighting it up, plus a more diffuse nebula. The image was made by combining many exposures taken through a mix of narrow and broad filters, which pick out light from particular gases as well as overall colour.
explore: The field of view is 248 by 332 arcseconds, which corresponds to roughly 200 by 270 light-years. North is up and east is to the left. The region is about 170,000 light-years from Earth.

understand.summary: This six-colour composite was taken with the SuSI2 camera on ESO's New Technology Telescope in visible light, using narrowband filters such as hydrogen-alpha, hydrogen-beta and oxygen alongside broadband ones. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Narrowband filters isolate the light of individual gases, and co-added exposures build up detail that an eye could not see.

alt: A large nebula at the bottom, a star cluster from upper left to centre, and a group of compact reddish nebulae at top right.

caption: The northwestern part of the Eagle Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Very bright young stars shine out of glowing gas in this Hubble view of the Eagle Nebula, also called Messier 16. Hubble looked at the region's northwestern side, far from its middle.

The stars and the gas are related. The stars formed from the same cloud of material and now belong to an open cluster, catalogued as NGC 6611. These energetic youngsters give off ultraviolet radiation, which makes the surrounding nebula glow.

The cluster was discovered in the mid-eighteenth century, but the fainter nebula took almost two more decades to be noticed, when Charles Messier recorded it. The most famous part of the Eagle Nebula, its tall columns of star-forming gas and dust known as the Pillars of Creation, lies outside the field. The pillars became famous through an earlier Hubble image. The nebula lies about 7,000 light-years away.
explore: Messier 16 is in Serpens Cauda, the Tail of the Serpent, between Aquila, Sagittarius and Ophiuchus. Amateur telescopes can show it too. A small one picks up broad faint patches of nebula, while a 30 cm instrument or bigger might show the dark pillars on a good night. Hubble's view relies on its 2.4-metre mirror.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys made this image. A near-infrared filter (F775W) is coloured red and a blue filter (F475W) is coloured blue, with a green channel filled in to complete the colour.
understand.eye: Exposures of an hour through one filter and 54 minutes through the other, including near-infrared light the eye cannot see, reveal far more than a visual observer would.

alt: Bright young stars embedded in glowing gas in the outer part of the Eagle Nebula.

caption: Herbig-Haro 502 in the Orion Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The whole frame is filled with the colourful glow of the Orion Nebula. Just left of centre, a star sits in a pinkish haze, and a narrow pink jet reaches away from it, with curved shock fronts to the upper right and lower left. This is the area around Herbig-Haro 502, a tiny piece of a vast stellar nursery.

The star is very young and still wrapped in the gas cloud it formed from. That leftover material may one day build planets. The material of our own Earth probably sat in a similar cocoon about five billion years ago.

The jet and arcs are the Herbig-Haro object. Newborn stars fling out gas at hundreds of kilometres per second, and where it strikes surrounding gas and dust it forms glowing shocks. These are thought to fade after a few thousand years, though they are often much larger than our Solar System.
explore: At only around 1500 light-years away, the Orion Nebula is one of the nearest star-forming regions to us. Young stars wrapped in their birth clouds are considered important enough that much Hubble observing time has been devoted to them, and studying them helps explain how the Universe developed and is still changing.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys used filters for glowing hydrogen (F658N, red), ionised oxygen (F502N, green) and yellow light (F550W, blue).
understand.eye: Narrowband filters isolate individual gases and exposures of up to 2000 seconds gather far more light than the eye, so the colours are a scientific mapping rather than the view in an eyepiece.

alt: A colourful glowing nebula with a young star in a pink haze left of centre and a narrow pink jet with curved shock fronts.

caption: The star-forming cloud RCW 34, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: A richly coloured cloud of gas fills this picture. It is RCW 34, a place where new stars are forming, in the southern constellation of Vela, the Sails. The image was taken with the FORS instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope in northern Chile.

RCW 34 is catalogued as an H II region. That name describes clouds of hydrogen gas lit up by hot, young stars. The energetic light from those stars knocks electrons off the hydrogen atoms, and when the atoms recapture them they give off a characteristic glow, strongest in red light.

Clouds like this are where stars begin. Dense pockets of gas and dust collapse under their own gravity, heat up and eventually ignite. Once the new stars shine, their light and winds start to reshape and clear the cloud that made them. The region is about 10,000 light-years away.

understand.summary: The VLT's FORS instrument captured this visible-light image through blue, visual, red and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The telescope's long exposures and a filter tuned to glowing hydrogen reveal colour and detail that would be far too faint for the eye.

alt: A richly coloured cloud of glowing gas with stars.

caption: The Toby Jug Nebula (IC 2220), imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: This picture shows the Toby Jug Nebula, known more formally as IC 2220, a glowing cloud of gas and dust about 1,200 light-years from Earth. It lies in the southern constellation of Carina, the Ship's Keel.

The Toby Jug is a reflection nebula. Unlike nebulae that glow because their own gas has been energised, a reflection nebula shines mostly because its dust grains scatter the light of a nearby star, much as fog lights up around a street lamp. In the Toby Jug, that light comes from a central star inside the cloud, catalogued as HD 65750.

Because the nebula borrows its light, its appearance depends on both the star and the dust around it. Fine dust grains tend to scatter blue light more readily than red, which is why many reflection nebulae look bluish in colour photographs.

understand.summary: The VLT's FORS1 instrument took this image through blue, visual, red, hydrogen-alpha and oxygen filters in visible light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The telescope's exposures collect far more light than the eye can, revealing a faint nebula that would be hard to see directly.

alt: A cloud of gas and dust lit from within by a central star.

caption: The outskirts of the Tarantula Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Bright, wispy structures glowing green fill this close-up of the Tarantula Nebula's outer edge. The green is a quirk of the processing. The wisps mark ionised hydrogen gas, which really glows red, but the chosen filters and colours make it look green.

The Tarantula sits in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a neighbouring galaxy about 170,000 light-years away. It is the brightest known nebula in our Local Group of galaxies and also its largest and most active star-forming region, around 650 light-years across.

Newborn stars in these clouds give off strong ultraviolet light that ionises the gas around them. The clouds will not last. Stellar winds and that same radiation will eventually blow them away, leaving clusters of stars like the Pleiades. Most of the light comes from a young, very bright cluster at the nebula's centre, just outside the field.
explore: The nebula is so luminous that, if it were within 1000 light-years of Earth, it would cast shadows on our planet. It also hosted supernova 1987A, the closest supernova seen since the telescope was invented, which was visible to the naked eye.
A version of this image was made by Judy Schmidt for the Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys took this image in visible and infrared light. The exact filter colours aren't published, but the caption notes that red-glowing hydrogen appears green here.
understand.eye: An eye would see this hydrogen as red rather than green, and the infrared part of the data is invisible to us.

alt: Bright green wispy clouds of gas scattered with stars at the edge of the Tarantula Nebula.

caption: The Boomerang Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Two smooth, diffuse lobes spread out in a bow-tie shape, laced with faint arcs and ghostly filaments. This is the Boomerang Nebula, a young planetary nebula 5,000 light-years away in Centaurus. No colder object has yet been found anywhere in the Universe.

A planetary nebula forms when a dying star casts off gas in the last stages of its life. In the Boomerang, a fierce wind appears to be blowing ultracold gas away from the dying star, and the rapid expansion has cooled the nebula to just 1 degree above absolute zero. That is colder even than the faint afterglow of the Big Bang.

The name came from astronomers who saw it in 1980 with a ground-based telescope in Australia and noticed a slight curve in the lobes. Hubble's sharper view suggests Bow Tie Nebula might have suited it better. Most planetary nebulae have bubble-like lobes. The Boomerang may simply be too young to have formed them.
explore: Its record low temperature was found in 1995 by Sahai and Nyman with Chile's 15-metre Swedish ESO Submillimetre Telescope. The central star has been shedding up to one-thousandth of a solar mass of material a year for 1500 years. The light we see is starlight reflected by dust.

understand.summary: Hubble recorded this image in visible light through a single green-yellow filter, with a 1000-second exposure. No colour mapping applies to a single-filter image.
understand.eye: A 1000-second exposure gathers far more light than the eye, revealing faint arcs and filaments no one could see directly.

alt: A bow-tie-shaped nebula with smooth diffuse lobes containing faint arcs and wispy filaments.

caption: The planetary nebula IC 4406, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: This nebula has an unusual, almost rectangular outline. It is IC 4406, a planetary nebula in the southern constellation Lupus, the Wolf, at a distance that is uncertain but possibly about 5,000 light-years.

A planetary nebula is the shell of gas a Sun-like star throws off late in its life. IC 4406 belongs to the bipolar kind, where material streams out in two opposite directions. Other bipolar nebulae, such as the Butterfly Nebula, show a prominent dark band of dust across the middle. In IC 4406 that dusty band is weaker, and the inside of the nebula looks more even.

The colours carry information. Different parts of the nebula glow in different hues because they differ in what they are made of and in their physical conditions. This picture was taken with the Very Large Telescope's Test Camera, and the frames were combined without further processing beyond basic cleaning.
explore: The image combines short blue, green-yellow and red exposures of a few minutes each. The field shown is 1.5 by 1.5 arcminutes, with north to the upper right and east to the upper left.

understand.summary: The VLT Test Camera took this visible-light image through B, V and R filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The camera gathered light over several minutes, recording a faint nebula in far more colour and detail than an eye could see.

alt: A planetary nebula with an almost rectangular outline, showing regions of different colours.

caption: Sharpless 2-296 in the Seagull Nebula, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: Wisps of gas and dust twist through this scene, where dark clouds and glowing red ones weave among bright stars. This is Sharpless 2-296, which makes up part of the wings of the Seagull Nebula.

The red glow comes from hydrogen gas lit up by hot young stars. Their intense light strips electrons from the hydrogen, and as the atoms settle back they shine with a characteristic red colour. Regions like this are called H II regions. The dark clouds, by contrast, are cold dust dense enough to block the light behind it.

The Seagull Nebula takes its name from its resemblance to a bird with outstretched wings. The region is a jumble of different kinds of objects packed into one patch of sky. It was taken at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile, using the Wide Field Imager camera mounted on the 2.2-metre MPG/ESO telescope.
explore: The nebula is about 3,500 light-years away. Its official short catalogue name is Sh 2-296, and the Seagull Nebula as a whole has its own formal entry in the IC catalogue.

understand.summary: The Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope recorded this visible-light image through several broadband filters and a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures and a hydrogen filter bring out faint red gas that the eye would barely register, if at all.

alt: Dark clouds and glowing red clouds of gas and dust winding among bright stars.

caption: The Orion A molecular cloud, imaged by ESO's VISTA telescope
story: Many young stars, and other objects usually hidden deep inside dusty clouds, shine out of this infrared view. Its subject is the Orion A molecular cloud, the closest large-scale star factory known, about 1,350 light-years from Earth.
The picture is part of the largest high-resolution infrared mosaic of Orion ever made, built from observations by VISTA, a survey telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory in northern Chile.

A molecular cloud is a cold, dense store of gas and dust where stars are born. In visible light, the dust in such a cloud blocks the view, so the youngest stars stay out of sight. Infrared light passes through dust much more easily, so a telescope like VISTA can look inside and count the newborn stars still wrapped in their birth clouds. Surveys like this let astronomers follow star formation across a whole cloud at once.

understand.summary: VISTA's VIRCAM camera captured this image in near-infrared light through J, H and Ks filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the human eye, so the stars inside this dust would be hidden to a naked-eye observer.

alt: An infrared view of a dusty cloud in Orion scattered with many young stars.

caption: The star-forming region LH 95 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This sharp Hubble image shows a star-forming region in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy neighbouring our own, about 150,000 light-years away. The region is catalogued as LH 95.

LH 95 holds an interesting mix of stars. Alongside young, massive stars, Hubble found a large number of low-mass infant stars living side by side with them. Hubble's sharp view lets these small, faint newborn stars be picked out one by one.

Massive stars are rare, hot and short-lived, while low-mass stars are common and faint. In LH 95 both kinds share the same young star-forming region, the massive stars and the small ones born together. Astronomers first showed the image in Prague, at the International Astronomical Union's 2006 General Assembly.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded this image in visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The faint infant stars here are far too dim and distant for any eye to pick out, and part of the data is near-infrared light we cannot see.

alt: A star-forming region crowded with small, faint young stars alongside young massive stars.

caption: The sky around VFTS 102 in the Tarantula Nebula, imaged by ESO's MPG/ESO 2.2-metre and VISTA telescopes
story: At the centre of this wide view lies the brilliant star VFTS 102. Around it spreads part of the Tarantula Nebula, a stellar nursery in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small neighbouring galaxy of the Milky Way.
No star has been found spinning faster than VFTS 102. The caption describes it as brilliant, and the gas and stars of the Tarantula Nebula spread out around it on all sides.

The picture blends visible-light and infrared images from two telescopes in Chile, the 2.2-metre MPG/ESO telescope at La Silla with its Wide Field Imager and the 4.1-metre VISTA infrared survey telescope at Paranal. Combining the two kinds of light gives a single view of the region around the star.

understand.summary: This composite combines visible-light images from the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope with near-infrared images from VISTA. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The infrared part of the image records light the eye cannot see, and long exposures reveal faint nebula far beyond naked-eye view.

alt: A wide view of part of the Tarantula Nebula with a brilliant star at the centre.

caption: The supernova remnant 1E 0102.2-7219 in the Small Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Just below the centre of this picture sits a greenish-blue shell of debris, the remains of an exploded star. It is the supernova remnant E0102, in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a dwarf galaxy near the Milky Way. In the upper right glows its neighbour N 76, a star-forming region in lavender and peach tones.

The two look different because they are made of different stuff. N 76 shines mainly with hydrogen, while E0102 is rich in oxygen and has almost no hydrogen or helium. One idea is that the star that exploded had blown away its outer hydrogen in a strong wind first. It may have been a Wolf-Rayet star.
At only about 2000 years old, E0102 is young. That lets astronomers study material from a massive star's core directly, learning how stars are built and how they enrich their surroundings.
explore: E0102 lies almost 50 light-years from the edge of N 76. Wolf-Rayet stars can be upward of 20 times the Sun's mass and tens of thousands of times as luminous, and they have strong winds throughout their lives.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged the region in 2003 through blue, visible, infrared and hydrogen filters, combined with oxygen-emission images from Wide Field Planetary Camera 2. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Filters that isolate the glow of particular gases, such as oxygen and hydrogen, bring out colour differences an eye would not see.

scaleExtra: The Small Magellanic Cloud lies roughly 210,000 light-years away, according to the caption.
alt: A greenish-blue shell of debris below centre, with lavender and peach glowing clouds at upper right.

caption: The Dark Wolf Nebula, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: Dark clouds form the silhouette of a wolf against a colourful backdrop of glowing gas. The resemblance has earned this cloud the nickname Dark Wolf Nebula. The shape is an illusion made by cold dust blocking the light from the glowing clouds behind it.

Dark nebulae like this are places where gas and dust are thick and cold enough to hide what lies beyond them. They are also where new stars are born, because in their densest parts material can collapse under gravity and eventually ignite. The nebula is catalogued as a star-forming region.

The image comes from the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile, a telescope designed to photograph large areas of sky in detail. It is a big picture, with 283 million pixels, which lets it capture both the broad outline of the wolf and fine detail in the surrounding glowing clouds.

understand.summary: The VLT Survey Telescope's OmegaCAM camera made this visible-light image through u, g, r and i filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The camera builds up faint glowing gas over long exposures, so the colourful backdrop would be far dimmer to the eye.

scaleExtra: The nebula is around 5300 light-years from Earth, according to ESO.
alt: A dark, wolf-shaped cloud of dust silhouetted against colourful glowing gas.

caption: Part of the bubble nebula Sh2-308, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Wispy, nebulous fringes mark the edge of a vast bubble of gas in this Hubble view. The bubble is Sh2-308, a nebula blown around a massive and violent star called EZ Canis Majoris, and Hubble captured only part of it.

EZ Canis Majoris is a Wolf-Rayet star, one of the brightest known of its type. It has used up its outer shell of hydrogen, laying bare deeper layers of heavier elements that burn intensely hot. The fierce radiation pouring out of it drives thick stellar winds, which push on the material around the star and sculpt it outwards.

The result is like blowing up a balloon. The star's former outer hydrogen layers form the skin of the bubble, and the flood of radiation from the centre plays the part of the air. The gas in the bubble is ionised hydrogen, a kind of glowing gas often found between the stars.
explore: This image is a parallel field. Hubble can point two cameras at neighbouring patches of sky at once, one on the main target and one next to it. The Advanced Camera for Surveys took this view while a second Hubble camera imaged another part of the nebula. The nebula is about 2000 light-years away.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded this visible-light image through filters isolating the glow of ionised oxygen and nitrogen. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The filters pick out light from particular glowing gases, showing faint structure an eye could not see.

alt: Wispy, nebulous fringes of a large gas bubble surrounding a star.

caption: A thin section of the supernova remnant SN 1006, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A delicate ribbon of gas floats across this Hubble picture, surrounded by white dots and small orange smudges. The ribbon is a very thin slice of SN 1006, the remnant of a star that exploded more than 1,000 years ago.

Around 1 May 1006, people from Africa to Europe to the Far East saw and recorded a new light in the sky. It was probably the brightest star humans have ever seen, outshining Venus and fainter only than the Moon. It could be seen in daytime for weeks and without a telescope for two and a half years or more. A white dwarf star in its final death throes was behind the explosion.

The remnant sits more than 14 degrees from the plane of our galaxy's disc, so few other objects crowd the view. Most of the white dots are stars in the Milky Way, and the orange smudges are distant background galaxies.
explore: The ribbon shows up only in the hydrogen-light filter and was given a red hue in the colour image. The hydrogen observations came from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, and the blue, yellow-green and near-infrared data from its Wide Field Planetary Camera 2.

understand.summary: This composite combines hydrogen-light images from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys with Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 images in blue, yellow-green and near-infrared light. The remnant, seen only in hydrogen light, is coloured red.
understand.eye: The ribbon is visible only through a filter isolating hydrogen light, and it is far too faint for the eye in any case.

alt: A thin, delicate ribbon of gas crossing a field of white stars and small orange background galaxies.

caption: The planetary nebula NGC 5189, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the planetary nebula NGC 5189, whose intricate structure looks like a giant, brightly coloured ribbon twisting through space. Hubble released it as a holiday-season image.

A planetary nebula has nothing to do with planets. The name dates back to early astronomers, whose small telescopes showed some of these objects as round discs rather like planets. In fact, a planetary nebula is the gas thrown off by a star similar to the Sun as it reaches the end of its life. The exposed core of the star is left at the centre, and its strong ultraviolet light makes the expelled gas glow.

NGC 5189 is described as a stellar eruption with an intricate structure, and Hubble's sharp view shows that complexity in detail, from the broad sweep of the ribbon to its finer twists. The image used several filters, including ones tuned to the glow of particular gases such as hydrogen, oxygen and sulphur.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 took this image in visible and near-infrared light, including filters for hydrogen, oxygen and sulphur emission. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Narrowband filters single out the glow of individual gases, so the colours show chemistry and structure an eye would not separate.

alt: A planetary nebula with an intricate, brightly coloured ribbon-like structure.

caption: The superbubble in the star-forming region N44, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope, Chandra and Spitzer
story: Blue, red and yellow blend in this view of the star-forming region LHA 120-N44 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, one of the Milky Way's small companion galaxies. At its heart lies the star cluster NGC 1929.

The massive stars in that cluster give off intense radiation, blow matter out at high speed as stellar winds, and live fast before exploding as supernovae. Together, the winds and supernova shock waves have hollowed out a huge cavity in the surrounding gas, called a superbubble.

Each colour shows a different kind of light. X-rays from NASA's Chandra, shown in blue, trace very hot gas. Infrared from NASA's Spitzer, in red, shows dust and cooler gas, and the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope's visible-light view, in yellow, shows the young stars and glowing clouds. Together they helped explain why N44 is so bright in X-rays. Supernova shocks hit the cavity walls, and hot material evaporates from them.
explore: The name LHA 120-N44 comes from a 1956 catalogue, put together by the American astronomer and astronaut Karl Henize, listing stars and nebulae in the Magellanic Clouds that shine in hydrogen-alpha light. The letter N marks it as a nebula, and it is often called simply N44.

understand.summary: This multi-telescope composite shows Chandra X-ray data in blue, Spitzer infrared data in red, and visible light from the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope in yellow.
understand.eye: X-rays and infrared light are both invisible to the human eye. Only the yellow part of this image shows light we could see.

alt: A colourful star-forming region with a large cavity outlined in blue, red and yellow.

caption: The nebula NGC 248 in the Small Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This glowing nebula is NGC 248, which lies inside the Small Magellanic Cloud, a companion galaxy of the Milky Way roughly 200,000 light-years from Earth. Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed it in September 2015.

NGC 248 is an emission nebula, a cloud of gas that shines on its own. In such nebulae, hot stars typically flood the gas with energetic light, which strips electrons from hydrogen atoms. As the atoms recapture them, the gas gives off light of its own, especially in the red glow of hydrogen.

The observations were part of a survey nicknamed SMIDGE. Its full title spells out its purpose, which is to investigate how dust and gas evolve in the Small Magellanic Cloud. NGC 248 was one of the targets Hubble looked at for that project, using its Advanced Camera for Surveys.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged the nebula in visible and near-infrared light, including a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The hydrogen filter and long exposures reveal a glow far too faint for the eye to see at this distance.

alt: A glowing nebula of gas in a neighbouring galaxy.

caption: The star-forming region NGC 2035, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Clouds of gas and dust twist into odd shapes, while on the left thin filaments trail across the region. This is NGC 2035, a lesser-known region of the Large Magellanic Cloud, one of the galaxies closest to our own.

NGC 2035 holds both the beginning and the end of stellar life. Hot new stars are being born inside the clouds, and as they switch on, their energetic light and winds sculpt the surrounding gas into their unusual forms. The filaments on the left were created by a supernova, the explosive death of a massive star.

Birth and death can sit side by side like this because the most massive stars live only briefly, so some can explode while others nearby are still forming. The Very Large Telescope's power allowed astronomers to explore this region in fine detail.

understand.summary: The VLT's FORS2 instrument captured this visible-light image through broadband B, V and R filters plus oxygen and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Filters isolating glowing oxygen and hydrogen, together with long exposures, show faint structure that an eye could not pick out.

alt: Twisting clouds of gas and dust with thin supernova filaments on the left.

caption: An outer part of the nebula Messier 43, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Several brilliant hot young stars shine in this close-up of an outer part of Messier 43, the Orion Nebula's little brother. Around even younger stars, still wrapped in dust, Hubble picks out curious features.

Messier 43 is sometimes called De Mairan's Nebula after its discoverer. Only a dark lane of dust separates it from the famous Orion Nebula, Messier 42. Both belong to the Orion molecular cloud complex, a huge stellar nursery that also includes the Horsehead Nebula and the Flame Nebula.

The complex is about 1,400 light-years away, one of the closest regions of massive star formation to Earth. That nearness has made it a favourite Hubble target for two decades, tracking how stellar winds shape clouds, studying young stars and finding elusive objects such as brown dwarfs. The new observations turn to a less-studied corner.
explore: The Horsehead Nebula is also catalogued as Barnard 33, and the Flame Nebula as NGC 2024. The image spans roughly 3.3 arcminutes of sky, with 1000-second exposures through each filter.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys combined a yellow filter (F555W), coloured blue, with a near-infrared filter (F814W), coloured red.
understand.eye: The red channel records near-infrared light we cannot see, and yellow light is shown as blue, so the colours differ from what an eye would perceive.

alt: Bright hot young stars amid clouds of gas and dust, with small features around dust-shrouded younger stars.

caption: The star-forming region Messier 78, imaged by ESO's VISTA telescope
story: Blue patches of reflected light, dark streams of dust and red jets fill this detailed view of Messier 78, a star-forming region in the constellation Orion, the Hunter.

Each feature has a different origin. The blue regions are dust clouds reflecting the light of hot young stars, in the same way that mist glows around a lamp. The dark streams are thicker dust that blocks the light from behind. The red jets are the most revealing, because they come from stars still in the process of forming, which fling out narrow streams of material as they grow.

The image was taken with VISTA, an infrared survey telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile. Infrared light can pass through dust that hides young stars at visible wavelengths, so VISTA can show jets and newborn stars that visible-light images miss.

understand.summary: VISTA's VIRCAM camera imaged Messier 78 in near-infrared light through Z, Y, J, H and Ks filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Most of this light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, which is why the jets and hidden stars would not be seen directly.

alt: Blue reflection nebulae, dark dust streams and red jets in a star-forming region.

caption: Filaments of the Vela supernova remnant, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: Pink clouds of gas stretch into thin and thick filaments that twist together like tentacles into an intricate web, with bright stars scattered among them. This is a small part of the Vela supernova remnant in the southern constellation of Vela.

The web is the wreckage of a massive star. Around eleven thousand years ago it exploded as a supernova, throwing off its outer layers. The blast also sent shock waves racing outward, and as they squeezed the surrounding gas they created the network of filaments. Astronomers call the debris of such blasts a supernova remnant.

At 800 light-years from Earth, the Vela remnant is one of the closest known. The image comes from OmegaCAM, the wide-field camera on the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory, which specialises in large visible-light images of the sky.
explore: This frame is only a small section of a much larger OmegaCAM image. The data come from the VPHAS+ survey, and one of the filters used is tuned to the red light of glowing hydrogen.

understand.summary: The VLT Survey Telescope's OmegaCAM camera recorded this visible-light image through u, g, r, i and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures and a hydrogen filter bring out filaments far too faint for the eye to see.

alt: Pink filaments of gas twisting into a web among bright stars.

caption: The Butterfly Nebula (NGC 6302), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Two broad, clumpy clouds in cream, yellow and orange spread from either side of a dark central lane, like the outstretched wings of a butterfly. This is NGC 6302, the Butterfly Nebula, in Hubble's optical view. The wings look nearly opaque, blocking most background stars.

The nebula is bipolar, with two lobes pushing out in opposite directions. The dark band forming the butterfly's body is a doughnut-shaped ring of dusty gas seen edge-on. It hides the central star, the ancient core of a Sun-like star, which powers the nebula and makes it glow.

That dusty doughnut may explain the whole shape. By stopping gas from escaping evenly in all directions, it could funnel material into the two wings. The colours trace chemistry. Orange comes from ionised nitrogen and hydrogen, red accents from ionised sulfur, and blue from hydrogen atoms.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 imaged the nebula in visible light through narrowband filters for hydrogen-beta (blue), hydrogen-alpha (cyan), ionised nitrogen (orange) and ionised sulfur (red).
understand.eye: Narrowband filters separate the light of individual elements, so the colours map chemistry rather than exactly what an eye would see.

alt: A butterfly-shaped nebula with a dark central dust lane and two broad clumpy wings in cream, yellow and orange against black space with a few pinkish stars.

caption: The Necklace Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A glowing ring hangs in space, dotted with dense, bright knots of gas like diamonds on a necklace, with a single bright dot at its centre. This is the Necklace Nebula, a planetary nebula found only recently, made of gas shed by an ordinary star much like the Sun. The ring is about two light-years across.

The central dot is really two stars, only a few million kilometres apart, whirling around each other in little more than a day. About 25 000 years ago one star swelled so much that it swallowed its companion. The smaller star kept orbiting inside the giant, spinning it up until much of its gaseous envelope flew off into space.
Most of that gas escaped along the star's equator, forming the ring. The knots are dense clumps within it, glowing because they absorb ultraviolet light from the central stars.
explore: For comparison, Mercury takes 88 days to orbit the Sun, so the central pair's orbit of just over a day is very fast. The nebula lies 15 000 light-years away in Sagitta, the Arrow, and is also catalogued as PN G054.2-03.4.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 captured the glow of hydrogen (shown in blue), oxygen (green) and nitrogen (red) in visible light.
understand.eye: Filters isolating single gases make each one a separate colour, which is not how an eye would see the blend of light.

alt: A glowing ring of gas dotted with bright knots, with a single bright dot in the centre.

caption: The H II region N119 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: This picture shows N119, a glowing cloud of gas in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a neighbouring galaxy about 170,000 light-years away. Its most unusual feature is a pronounced spiral shape that recalls a barred spiral galaxy, even though N119 is a nebula, not a galaxy.

N119 is an H II region, a cloud of hydrogen gas lit by hot young stars. Their energetic light strips electrons from the hydrogen atoms, and the gas glows as the atoms recapture them. The image includes a filter tuned to that hydrogen glow.

The nebula is large and sits in an interesting place. It lies on the northern side of the Large Magellanic Cloud's stellar bar, a long band of stars across the galaxy, close to the centre around which the galaxy's neutral hydrogen rotates. That bar is also why the lower half of the field is packed with many more stars than the upper half.
explore: N119 measures about 400 by 600 light-years. The image was made with the Wide Field Imager through blue, visual and hydrogen-alpha filters.

understand.summary: The Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope took this visible-light image through B, V and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The hydrogen filter and long exposures reveal glowing gas far too faint for the eye to see.

alt: A glowing nebula with a spiral shape among many stars, denser in the lower half.

caption: The Herbig–Haro objects HH 7–11 in NGC 1333, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Five small objects glow blue near the top centre of this image. They are the Herbig–Haro objects HH 7 to 11, a smoking gun left by a newborn star, and they sit inside NGC 1333, a dusty, gas-rich reflection nebula.

Herbig–Haro objects form when a young star shoots out jets of ionised gas that crash into nearby clouds at high speed. These five were made by jets from the young star SVS 13, and the collisions produced five bright clumps of light in the nebula. Each of them is heading up and to the left, away from their parent star.

They will not last. Racing outward at up to 250 000 kilometres per hour, such objects fade away within a few tens of thousands of years, a short time for astronomers. HH 7 is now about 20 000 times as far from SVS 13 as Earth is from the Sun.
explore: NGC 1333 lies about a thousand light-years from Earth. A reflection nebula shines by scattering the light of nearby stars off its dust.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys took this image through visible and near-infrared filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and these small faint clumps would be invisible without a large telescope.

alt: Five small blue glowing clumps near the top centre of a dusty nebula.

caption: The nebula NGC 3199, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: A crescent-shaped cocoon of gas and dust seems to plough through a star-studded sky, like a ship in stormy seas. The comparison suits its location. NGC 3199 lies in Carina, a southern constellation named after the keel of a ship, about 12,000 light-years from Earth.

Inside the nebula is HD 89358, an extremely hot and massive Wolf-Rayet star. It drives fierce stellar winds and outflows that crash into the surrounding material and sweep it up, which helps give NGC 3199 its twisted, lopsided look. Astronomers now know the bright crescent belongs to a far bigger, dimmer bubble of gas and dust.

John Herschel discovered the nebula in 1834 while compiling his catalogue of interesting night-sky objects. Since then it has been observed many times, including with ESO's 8.2-metre Very Large Telescope. This image comes from its smaller neighbour, the 2.6-metre VLT Survey Telescope.
explore: The VST began operations in 2011. Its 256-megapixel camera, OmegaCAM, can photograph an area of sky twice the size of the full Moon at once. That lets it survey interesting objects which the Very Large Telescope can then study in even more detail.

understand.summary: The VLT Survey Telescope's OmegaCAM camera recorded this visible-light image through g, r and i filters and a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures and a hydrogen filter reveal faint gas that would be almost invisible to the eye.

alt: A crescent-shaped cloud of gas and dust moving across a field packed with stars.

caption: The supernova remnant DEM L316A, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Rippling wisps of ionised gas spread across this Hubble image. They are DEM L316A, the remains of a long-dead star, lying some 160 000 light-years away in the Large Magellanic Cloud, one of the Milky Way's nearest galactic neighbours.

The star died in an especially bright and energetic kind of explosion called a Type Ia supernova. These are thought to happen when a white dwarf pulls more material from a close companion star than it can handle and becomes unstable. The result is a violent blast that hurls the star's outer layers into space at immense speeds.

As that expelled gas ploughs through the material between the stars, it heats it and ionises it, meaning electrons are stripped from the atoms. This creates the faint glow recorded by Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3.
explore: The Large Magellanic Cloud is a satellite of the Milky Way and the fourth-largest galaxy in the Local Group. Hubble has imaged other supernova remnants there too, including SNR 0509 in 2010 and SNR 0519 in 2013.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 imaged the remnant in visible and near-infrared light, including a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The glow is faint and partly in near-infrared light, so an eye would not see these wisps.

alt: Rippling wisps of glowing gas from an exploded star.

caption: The young star SSTC2D J033038.2+303212, reflection nebula [B77] 63 and dark nebula Dobashi 4173, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Near the upper middle, surrounded by bright stars, a small young star appears to push a murky chimney of material down and out, with bright gas bursting around it. Below it, a bright wispy cloud appears to spew a dark stream of smoke into space. Several kinds of objects share this Hubble frame.
The small star, catalogued as SSTC2D J033038.2+303212, is still forming. A bright disc of material swirls around it, which we see edge-on.

The bright cloud is [B77] 63, a reflection nebula shining with light from stars inside it, notably the emission-line star LkHA 326 and a close neighbour. These stars light up and sculpt the gas. The dark stream is Dobashi 4173, a dark nebula dense enough to hide the sky behind it, creating what look like empty rips in space. The stars that appear on top of that blackness actually lie between us and the cloud.
explore: Among the stars lighting [B77] 63, the most notable is LkHA 326, an emission-line star with another star sitting very close beside it. Dark nebulae like Dobashi 4173 are extremely dense clouds of material that block background light.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys took this image through visible and near-infrared filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the faint wisps need long exposures to show up.

alt: A small young star with a dark chimney of material near the top, and a bright wispy cloud with a dark stream of dust at the bottom.

caption: The planetary nebula NGC 1514, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: What looks like one bright star with purple spikes sits in the middle of a tilted, diffuse cylinder of gas and dust. It is actually two stars. Around them is a bright pink, clumpy cloud, and two large rings, which appear joined at top left and bottom right, are orange in those places and blue at the bottom and centre right. This is the planetary nebula NGC 1514.

A planetary nebula is the gas cast off by a Sun-like star near the end of its life. Webb's mid-infrared view is the most detailed image of this one so far. It shows the rings as fuzzy, intricate clumps of dust rather than smooth bands.
Webb also reveals more clearly the holes that pierce the bright pink core. The rings have denser edges that bend inward in shallow V shapes. The nebula is about 1,500 light-years away.
explore: Tiny stars and galaxies, mostly blue and yellow, speckle the black background. Webb did not observe strips along the top edges, a thin vertical line near the nebula at top left, or the bottom left and right corners.

understand.summary: Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI) captured this image through three mid-infrared filters, shown as blue (7.7 microns), yellow (12 microns) and red (25 microns).
understand.eye: Mid-infrared light is invisible to the human eye, so these rings of dust would not look like this to a viewer.

alt: A bright double star with purple diffraction spikes inside a diffuse cylinder of gas, with a pink clumpy centre and two crossing rings in orange and blue.

caption: The supernova remnant DEM L71, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Separate fiery filaments are scattered across this Hubble scene. They are the shrapnel of a star that exploded several thousand years ago, some 160 000 light-years away in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a galaxy close to our own. The remnant is called DEM L71.

The star that exploded was a white dwarf, the dense leftover core of a star. Most stars in the Milky Way with masses from a tenth of the Sun's up to eight times it are expected to end up this way. A white dwarf in a binary can siphon gas from a close companion. If it takes more than it can handle, it turns unstable and blows up in what is called a Type Ia supernova.

That is what happened to the star behind DEM L71. The white dwarf ripped itself apart, flinging out a superheated cloud of debris. As the debris slammed into the surrounding gas, it slowly spread into the filaments.
explore: Around 97% of stars in that mass range are expected to become white dwarfs. Before it blows up, the white dwarf is thought to grow until it is about half again as large as the Sun. Supernovae are among the brightest events ever observed.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 imaged the remnant in visible and near-infrared light, including a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: These faint filaments, partly recorded in near-infrared light, would be invisible to the eye.

alt: Scattered fiery filaments of material from an exploded star.

caption: The star-forming nebula RCW 36, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Clouds strewn across this picture are thick enough in places to block the light behind them, leaving patches and wisps of inky black. This is RCW 36, also called Gum 20, an emission nebula in the constellation Vela, the Sails. At about 2,300 light-years away, it is among the nearest places to our Solar System where massive stars are forming.

Those dark clouds may look lifeless, but they are exactly where stars form. Inside them, clumps of dust and molecular hydrogen fall inward and pull together into new stars, which can end up with small families of planets around them, like our own Solar System.

RCW 36 is only one part of a larger star-forming complex known as the Vela Molecular Ridge. The picture was taken with FORS, an instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope that combines a camera with a spectrograph.
explore: This image was produced by ESO's Cosmic Gems programme, which uses telescope time that cannot be used for science to make outreach images of interesting objects. The data are also placed in ESO's science archive, where astronomers can use them.

understand.summary: The VLT's FORS2 instrument took this visible-light image through broadband filters and filters for oxygen and hydrogen-alpha emission. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures and gas-specific filters bring out faint glowing gas that the eye could not see.

alt: Glowing clouds with patches and wisps of inky black dust.

caption: The supernova remnant SNR 0454-67.2, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Threads of red snake through dark, turbulent clouds in this tangled web. It is SNR 0454-67.2, a supernova remnant, the debris of a massive star that ended its life in a huge explosion and threw its material into surrounding space.

The remnant sits in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small spiral galaxy neighbouring the Milky Way. It probably came from a Type Ia supernova. In this kind of explosion a white dwarf star keeps pulling material from a companion star until it reaches a critical mass, and then it blows apart.

Type Ia supernovae matter far beyond this one messy cloud. Because they happen in the same specific way, when the white dwarf reaches a particular mass, they always have a well-known brightness. That makes them useful as standard candles. By comparing how bright one looks with how bright it really is, scientists can measure distances across the Universe.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 imaged the remnant in visible and near-infrared light, including a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The faint glowing threads need long exposures and are partly recorded in near-infrared light, so the eye would not see them.

alt: Threads of red winding through dark, turbulent clouds.

caption: The young star IRAS 14568-6304 in the Circinus molecular cloud, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A young star wrapped in a haze of golden gas and dust sits within a sweeping curve of darkness that hides the sky behind it. The star is IRAS 14568-6304, and a tail extends below it. The dark swoosh is the Circinus molecular cloud.

That cloud holds around 250 000 times the Sun's mass in gas, dust and young stars. Two huge clumps within it, nicknamed Circinus-West and Circinus-East, are its leading star-forming sites. IRAS 14568-6304 lies under a blurry fog inside Circinus-West.

The tail is a protostellar jet. Most of the material a new star gathers from its parent cloud goes into the star and its accretion disc, which may one day form planets. But at some stage the star began flinging some of it into space at supersonic speeds. Jets like this give astronomers valuable clues about how stars form.
explore: Each of the two big clumps holds roughly 5000 solar masses. Several stars in Circinus-West drive outflows, IRAS 14568-6304 among them, and together they form an outflow ranking among the most energetic, most massive and brightest yet reported. Some scientists have suggested calling Circinus-West the nest of molecular outflows. Serge Meunier entered a version of this image in the Hubble's Hidden Treasures competition.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged this region through visible and near-infrared filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the faint golden haze would be far too dim to see directly.

alt: A young star in a golden haze of gas and dust with a tail below it, set in a curving band of dark cloud.

caption: The expanding bubble of Tycho's Supernova, imaged by the Chandra X-ray Observatory
story: This wide view shows the region around Tycho's Supernova, where the explosion's hot, expanding bubble shows up in X-rays. The picture comes from NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory, and its lower edge is clipped because the remnant's southern end lay beyond what the camera could see.

A supernova remnant is the cloud of debris and heated gas left after a star explodes. As the blast wave sweeps outward it heats material to extremely high temperatures, hot enough to shine in X-rays rather than just in visible light.

The colours here are not what an eye would see. Instead they sort the X-rays by energy, with red marking low-energy X-rays, green medium and blue high. The remnant is about 10,000 light-years away in the constellation Cassiopeia.

understand.summary: This is an X-ray image from the Chandra X-ray Observatory, with red, green and blue representing low, medium and high X-ray energies.
understand.eye: X-rays are completely invisible to the human eye, and they are blocked by Earth's atmosphere, so this view can only come from space.

alt: An expanding bubble of hot gas shown in red, green and blue, cut off along the bottom edge.

caption: A group of stars in the reflection nebula NGC 1333, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A small handful of stars, just about enough to make up a football team, shines out of the gas and dust in this Hubble view. They belong to NGC 1333, the cloud that formed them and that they still call home.

About 1,000 light-years from us, NGC 1333 sits in Perseus, the constellation known as the Hero. The cool gas and dust gathered here are still producing new stars. Their light bounces off the surrounding material and lights it up, which is how we can see the cloud at all. That is why NGC 1333 is classified as a reflection nebula.

Reflection nebulae shine with borrowed light. Instead of glowing on their own, their dust grains scatter starlight toward us. Only one region of NGC 1333 is covered. Earlier, wider Hubble images show that this small team is just one of many groups of young stars across the nebula.
explore: Our galaxy hosts around 300 billion stars, so the handful caught here is a tiny sample. This team-sized group is only one gathering among many in NGC 1333.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged the region through visible and near-infrared filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of this light is near-infrared, invisible to us, and the faint reflected glow needs long exposures to show up.

alt: A handful of stars embedded in clouds of gas and dust.

caption: The Butterfly Nebula (NGC 6302), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows NGC 6302, better known as the Butterfly Nebula, a glowing cloud of gas within our Milky Way in the constellation of Scorpius.

The glowing gas once formed the outer layers of a star. Over about 2,200 years it has been cast off into space, building the butterfly shape. The nebula is a planetary nebula, the name astronomers give to gas thrown off by a Sun-like star near the end of its life. Despite the name, planetary nebulae have nothing to do with planets.

New observations have revealed unprecedented complexity in the nebula, and the jets and gas bubbles streaming from the star at its centre are changing quickly. The image uses several filters, including ones in near-infrared light and others tuned to the glow of particular gases.
explore: From wingtip to wingtip the butterfly spans over two light-years, roughly half the gap between the Sun and Proxima Centauri, our nearest stellar neighbour.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 imaged the nebula in visible and near-infrared light, using filters for oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen and iron emission. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Several filters isolate single gases and some record near-infrared light, so the colours represent chemistry rather than what the eye would see.

scaleExtra: The nebula lies roughly 3800 light-years away, according to the caption.
alt: A glowing, butterfly-shaped nebula with jets and bubbles of gas.

caption: The Gum 3 nebula, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: Red and pink clouds mix with blue in this bright view of the Gum 3 nebula, and part of it resembles a koi fish. Just to the right of the brightest region, the pink fish, a patch of sky seems oddly empty of stars.

Each colour has its own cause. Intense ultraviolet light from nearby young stars strikes hydrogen atoms in the cloud, which then give off visible light at very specific colours, which appear as reds and pinks. Tiny dust particles also reflect starlight, especially blue light, for the same reason Earth's sky looks blue.

The empty-looking patch is not really short of stars. A large knot of dust sits there, soaking up visible light and screening the stars beyond it. Gum 3 is a cloud of gas and dust between the constellations Monoceros and Canis Major, named after the Australian astronomer Colin Stanley Gum.
explore: Gum catalogued 84 nebulae in the southern sky. The picture was taken with the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory, whose OmegaCAM camera has 268 megapixels and is built to map wide swathes of the southern sky in visible light.

understand.summary: The VLT Survey Telescope's OmegaCAM camera took this visible-light image. The filter details and colour mapping aren't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures gather far more light than the eye, so these colours would appear much fainter, if at all, to a viewer.

alt: A brightly coloured nebula of red, pink and blue clouds, part shaped like a koi fish, with a dark, star-poor patch beside it.

caption: The star-forming region Gum 26, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: A faint pinkish glow fills this view of Gum 26, a star-forming region found in Vela, the Sails, a constellation of the southern sky. It was imaged by the FORS instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope in Chile.

Our galaxy contains many places like this, where new stars spring to life inside collapsing clumps of gas and dust. Gum 26 is an HII region, or emission nebula. Newly formed stars stream out intense ultraviolet radiation that ionises the hydrogen gas around them, and that ionised gas gives off the pink glow.

Catching young stars pink-handed in this way is useful. By studying the glowing gas, astronomers can learn about the conditions in which stars form, and study how the newcomers then influence their surroundings.
explore: The image was made through ESO's Cosmic Gems programme, which uses telescope time unsuitable for science to create outreach images. Its data also go into ESO's science archive for astronomers.

understand.summary: The VLT's FORS2 instrument captured this visible-light image through B, V and R filters and a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: A hydrogen filter and long exposures bring out a faint pink glow that the eye would struggle to see.

caption: The planetary nebula IC 1295, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: A glowing green nebula surrounds a dim, dying star in this picture from ESO's Very Large Telescope. The object is the planetary nebula IC 1295, about 3,300 light-years from us in Scutum, a constellation whose name means the Shield. According to ESO, no more detailed picture of it has been taken.

A planetary nebula forms near the end of a Sun-like star's life. The star sheds its outer layers into space, leaving behind its hot core. Ultraviolet light from that core then makes the expelled gas glow. The name is a historical accident. Through early telescopes such objects looked round like planets, but they have nothing to do with them.
The faint star at the centre is what remains of the original star. Described as dim and dying, it is the source of the light that sets the green shell glowing around it.

understand.summary: The VLT's FORS1 instrument took this visible-light image through B, V and R filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The camera gathers far more light than the eye, so the nebula's green glow would be much fainter to a viewer.
