caption: The emission nebula IC1284 and reflection nebulae NGC6589 and NGC6590, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: A large, bright nebula glows rosy red in the centre of this picture, while blue nebulae sit in the lower right corner. The two colours mark two different kinds of nebula.

The red one is IC1284, a star-forming region made mostly of hydrogen. Radiation from young stars excites the electrons in the hydrogen atoms. As they settle back and lose energy, they give off light at one specific reddish wavelength. One of the camera's filters lets through exactly this colour, which gives the nebula its look.

The blue ones, NGC6589 and NGC6590, are reflection nebulae, highlighted by a different filter. Their dust scatters the shorter, bluer wavelengths from nearby stars more than the red, which gives them an eerie glow. It's the same reason our daytime sky is blue. The image was taken with OmegaCAM on the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory.
explore: The frame covers an area of sky roughly the size of a full Moon. It is part of VPHAS+, a large public ESO survey that records stars and nebulae in visible light, with the aim of learning how stars are born, how they live and how they die.

understand.summary: The VLT Survey Telescope's OmegaCAM camera took this visible-light image through u, g, r and i filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter. The caption notes one filter captures the red hydrogen glow and another highlights the blue nebulae, but the full colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal both nebulae much more strongly than the eye could see them.

alt: A large rosy-red nebula in the centre and small blue nebulae in the lower right corner.

caption: The RCW 94 and RCW 95 nebulae, imaged by ESO's VLT Survey Telescope and VISTA
story: A cloud of gas and dust spreads across this image in the shape of a bat, glowing an intense red. The most prominent clouds are RCW 94, forming the bat's right wing, and RCW 95, forming its body. The rest of the bat has not been given a formal name.

The red glow comes from hydrogen. Young stars inside the cloud give off intense radiation that strips electrons from hydrogen atoms, and the ionised gas shines in response. Clouds like these are where stars are born.

Most of the data are visible-light observations by the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile, combined with extra infrared data from VISTA, the Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy, also at Paranal.

understand.summary: This combines visible-light data from the VLT Survey Telescope with infrared data from VISTA. The filters and colour mapping aren't published.
understand.eye: The infrared part of the data is invisible to the eye, and the red glow is gathered through long exposures.

alt: A bat-shaped cloud of gas and dust glowing intense red.

caption: The RCW 36 nebula, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Dark clouds in the middle form the head and body of what looks like a hawk, with filaments to the left and right as outstretched wings. Below it lies a bright blue nebula lit by massive newborn stars, whose intense radiation makes the surrounding gas glow. This is the RCW 36 nebula in the constellation Vela.

Fittingly, the hawk-like nebula was captured by HAWK-I, an instrument on the Very Large Telescope. The astronomers were most interested in faint, hidden objects called brown dwarfs, which cannot fuse hydrogen in their cores.

HAWK-I suits this job. It works at infrared wavelengths, where cold failed stars are easier to spot, and uses adaptive optics to correct for atmospheric turbulence, producing sharp images. Lead author Afonso do Brito do Vale likened the massive stars clearing away their clouds to an animal breaking out of its eggshell.
explore: Do Brito do Vale is a doctoral student working between a research institute in Portugal and an astrophysics laboratory in Bordeaux, France. The image appeared in a new paper, and the study should help explain how brown dwarfs form.

understand.summary: The VLT's HAWK-I instrument imaged RCW 36 in near-infrared light through J, H and Ks filters, with adaptive optics. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the dim brown dwarfs astronomers sought would not be seen directly.

scaleExtra: The nebula is about 2300 light-years away, according to ESO.
alt: Dark hawk-shaped clouds with filament wings above a bright blue glowing nebula containing young stars.

caption: The cometary globule GN 16.43.7.01, the Dark Tower, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: A dusty head trails a long, dark tail in this picture, its outline traced by a pink glow. The object is a cometary globule catalogued as GN 16.43.7.01 and nicknamed the Dark Tower. About 5,000 light-years away, it sits in Scorpius, the Scorpion, a constellation of the southern sky.

Despite the name, cometary globules have nothing to do with comets. They are named only for their look, with a dense head and a stretched-out tail. Inside this one are thick clumps of gas and dust that are collapsing, and out of which new stars will be born.

Its strange shape is sculpted from outside. A cluster of young, bright stars lies out of view to the upper left, and their intense radiation pounds the globule, carving it into a tower. The same radiation wraps around its edges, lighting them with the pink glow typical of hot, excited gas. The picture was taken with the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile.
explore: The globule is classified as a Bok globule, a small, dense, dark cloud of gas and dust. Astronomers often give objects with odd catalogue names obvious nicknames, such as the Dark Tower.

understand.summary: The VLT Survey Telescope took this visible-light image. The filters and colour mapping aren't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal the faint pink rim of glowing gas, which would be too dim for the eye.

alt: A dark, tower-like cloud with a dusty head and elongated tail, outlined by a pink glow.

caption: The dark nebulae Barnard 92 and Barnard 93, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: Two dark, wispy clouds hang against a field of stars, like ghostly trails in the sky. They are Barnard 92, on the right, and Barnard 93, on the left, two dark nebulae photographed from ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile.

Their inky darkness comes from thick gas and dust that block the light of the stars behind. That darkness hides activity, because these clouds are stellar nurseries, where collapsing gas and dust give birth to new stars.

The rich starry backdrop is part of a much larger complex, the Small Sagittarius Star Cloud, also catalogued by Charles Messier as Messier 24. This part of the sky, in the constellation Sagittarius, is so crowded with stars that it can be seen with the naked eye on dark nights.
explore: The image was taken with OmegaCAM, a 268-million-pixel camera on the VLT Survey Telescope designed for wide fields. This field could hold four full Moons. It is part of the VPHAS+ survey, which has mapped diffuse nebulae and both young and evolved stars in our galaxy.

understand.summary: The VLT Survey Telescope's OmegaCAM camera took this visible-light image through g, r and i filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The star cloud is visible to the naked eye on dark nights, but the camera records far more stars and detail than the eye could.

alt: Two dark, wispy clouds silhouetted against a field of stars.

caption: The faint halo of the Cat's Eye Nebula, imaged by the Nordic Optical Telescope
story: An enormous but extremely faint halo of gas surrounds the Cat's Eye Nebula in this picture, reaching more than three light-years across. Oxygen shows in blue and nitrogen in red. The Cat's Eye is a planetary nebula, the gas shed by a Sun-like star late in its life.

In recent years, astronomers have found that some planetary nebulae have halos like this. They probably formed from material thrown off during earlier active episodes in the star's life, probably between 50,000 and 90,000 years ago.

Seeing such a faint structure takes a long look through filters that isolate individual gases. Romano Corradi took the exposures at the Nordic Optical Telescope, which stands on La Palma in the Canary Islands, using two narrow-band exposures of 1800 seconds each. The halo acts as a record of the star's past, preserving material it lost long ago.
explore: The Cat's Eye Nebula is also catalogued as NGC 6543 and lies about 3,000 light-years away in the constellation Draco. Each of the two narrow-band exposures lasted 1800 seconds.

understand.summary: The Nordic Optical Telescope recorded this visible-light image through two narrow-band filters, with oxygen shown in blue and nitrogen in red.
understand.eye: The halo is far too faint for the eye. Half-hour exposures through gas-specific filters were needed to bring it out.

alt: A bright planetary nebula surrounded by an enormous, very faint halo of gas in blue and red.

caption: The nebula SBW1 and its giant star, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A lidless purple eye seems to stare back from the centre of this Hubble image. It is a nebula known officially as [SBW2007] 1, nicknamed SBW1, with a giant star at its heart. The star was born about twenty times as massive as the Sun and now sits inside a swirling ring of purple gas.
That ring is left over from an earlier era, when the star threw off its outer layers through violent pulsations and winds. Scientists say the star is destined to explode as a supernova.

It closely resembles the star behind SN 1987A, a famous supernova. Early Hubble images of that explosion show a ring of the same size and age as SBW1's, moving at a similar speed. Both stars also sat in similar HII regions and had the same brightness. SBW1 is like a snapshot of SN 1987A before it blew up, so astronomers study the two together.
explore: SBW1 lies over 20 000 light-years away, so its eventual explosion will pose no danger to watchers here, and if we are lucky it may happen within our lifetimes. Nick Rose and Steve Byrne entered versions of this image in the Hubble's Hidden Treasures competition.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 imaged SBW1 through visible-light filters, including ones near the hydrogen-alpha and nitrogen wavelengths. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The ring's glow is faint and was isolated with narrow filters, so an eye would not see it like this.

alt: A purple ring of gas resembling an eye, with a giant star at its centre.

caption: The stellar nursery N159 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Glowing gas and dark dust swirl together like a storm in this Hubble shot. The scene is N159, a stellar nursery in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. It is an HII region over 150 light-years across.

Many hot young stars live in N159. Their intense ultraviolet light makes the nearby hydrogen gas glow, while their fierce stellar winds carve the surrounding material into ridges, arcs and filaments. The stormy look is the stars reshaping the cloud they formed in.

At the heart of the cloud lies the Papillon Nebula, a small, dense, butterfly-shaped patch of glowing gas. It is classed as a High-Excitation Blob, a kind of object thought to be closely tied to how massive stars begin to form.
explore: N159 is more than 160,000 light-years away, just south of the Tarantula Nebula, another large star-forming complex in the same galaxy. Hubble's earlier Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 imaged N159 before and was the first to resolve the Papillon Nebula.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged N159 through visible and near-infrared filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and the nebula is far too faint to see in this detail.

alt: Swirling glowing gas and dark dust forming ridges, arcs and filaments.

caption: The star-forming region LHA 120-N11 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Gas clouds lit in a mix of colours fill this Hubble image of LHA 120-N11, a star-forming region in the Large Magellanic Cloud. That small galaxy is a satellite of the Milky Way, circling ours in a long, slow orbit.

The Milky Way's gravity gently tugs on its neighbour's gas clouds. As they are pulled, some of them collapse and form new stars. Those young stars then light up the clouds around them in many colours.

A star-forming region is a place where clouds of gas and dust gather, collapse and give rise to new stars. In N11, the process is linked to the long gravitational relationship between the two galaxies, as the larger one's pull stirs up the gas of the smaller. The region is also catalogued as NGC 1769.
explore: The image combines several filters, from blue light to near-infrared, and includes one that isolates the red glow of hydrogen gas.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged the region through blue, visual, red, hydrogen-alpha and near-infrared filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures, a hydrogen filter and near-infrared light reveal colours the eye could not see.

caption: The Sh2-54 nebula, imaged by ESO's VISTA telescope
story: Stars shine through the clouds of the Sh2-54 nebula in this infrared view. It was taken with ESO's VISTA telescope at Paranal Observatory in Chile.

The Sh2-54 nebula shows just how much the kind of light matters. In visible light, the dust and gas of Sh2-54 are obvious. In infrared light those clouds become much less noticeable, and the light of stars behind the nebula pierces through.

This happens because infrared light has longer wavelengths than visible light and passes through dust far more easily. Astronomers use this to look inside and behind dusty regions, spotting stars that would otherwise be hidden. Comparing infrared and visible views of the same nebula helps them build a fuller picture of what the cloud contains.

understand.summary: VISTA's VIRCAM camera imaged the nebula in near-infrared light through J, H and Ks filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and an eye would see the dusty clouds rather than the stars behind them.

alt: Stars shining through the clouds of a nebula in infrared light.

caption: The Horsehead Nebula, imaged by the Callisto telescope of the SPECULOOS Southern Observatory
story: The famous Horsehead Nebula appears in the very first image taken by Callisto, one of the telescopes of the SPECULOOS Southern Observatory. A first light is the first image a newly commissioned telescope takes, and well-known objects like this are often chosen to mark the occasion.
The Horsehead is a dark nebula, a thick cloud of dust that blocks the light from behind it, so it shows up as a silhouette.

SPECULOOS has a different main job. It is made up of four 1-metre telescopes built to hunt for planets, and they are named after Jupiter's Galilean moons, of which Callisto is one. The observatory will look for planets the size of Earth around nearby brown dwarfs and ultra-cool stars. The telescopes sit at ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile's Atacama Desert, near the Very Large Telescope and VISTA.

understand.summary: The Callisto telescope took this image through visible and near-infrared filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The Horsehead is too faint to see with the naked eye. A camera exposure gathers enough light to reveal its outline.

alt: The Horsehead Nebula, a dark horse-head-shaped cloud.

caption: The Eta Carinae star system in ultraviolet light, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Two dusty bubbles bulge out in opposite directions, wrapped in blue glowing gas and edged with red filaments. This is the nebula around Eta Carinae, a star system prone to violent outbursts. The bubbles were formed by material ejected during one such episode in the 1840s.

This view uses ultraviolet light, captured by Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3. It revealed the glow of magnesium in warm gas, shown in blue, in places astronomers had not seen it before. The magnesium lies between the dusty bubbles and the outer filaments, which are rich in nitrogen and heated by shocks, shown in red.

The blue region outside the lower-left bubble is crossed by streaks. They form where the star's light pokes through clumps of dust on the bubble's surface. Where ultraviolet light hits the dense dust, it casts a long, thin shadow out into the surrounding gas.
explore: Telescopes including Hubble have monitored the Eta Carinae system for more than two decades. The outburst that produced the two bubbles took place in the 1840s.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed in ultraviolet and visible light. Magnesium glow in warm gas is shown in blue and nitrogen-rich filaments in red.
understand.eye: Much of this light is ultraviolet, which the eye cannot see and which Earth's atmosphere blocks.

scaleExtra: Eta Carinae lies 7500 light-years away, according to the caption.
alt: Two dusty bipolar bubbles surrounded by blue glowing gas with streaks and outer red filaments.

caption: The star-forming region LHA 120-N 180B, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: This picture shows a region of newly forming stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy near the Milky Way. It was captured by MUSE, the Multi Unit Spectroscopic Explorer, an instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope.

MUSE is more than a camera. For every point in its field it records a full spectrum, splitting the light into its many colours. That lets astronomers map which gases are glowing where. The picture was built from the light of oxygen, hydrogen and sulphur.

The Large Magellanic Cloud has relatively little dust, which makes it easier to see into its star-forming regions. Combined with MUSE's sharp vision, that allowed intricate details of this region to be picked out in visible light. The region is catalogued as LHA 120-N 180B.

understand.summary: The VLT's MUSE instrument observed this region in visible light, and the image uses the emission of oxygen, hydrogen-alpha and sulphur. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Selecting single wavelengths of glowing gas from MUSE's spectra brings out structure the eye would not separate.

alt: A region of glowing gas clouds with newly forming stars.

caption: The supernova remnant SNR 0519, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Thin, blood-red shells made of delicate wisps of gas curve through this Hubble image. Together they form SNR B0519-69.0, usually shortened to SNR 0519, the debris of a star whose supernova explosion happened around 600 years ago.

There are several kinds of supernova. In this case, astronomers know the exploding star was a white dwarf, the dense leftover core of a Sun-like star in the last stage of its life. The unstable star exploded violently, and these thin shells are what remains.

SNR 0519 lies more than 150,000 light-years away in the southern constellation Dorado, the Dolphinfish. That constellation also holds most of the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, so this part of the sky is crowded with interesting deep-sky objects. The remnant sits within that neighbouring galaxy.
explore: The Large Magellanic Cloud is the fourth largest galaxy in our Local Group. Hubble has seen a similar remnant there, SNR B0509-67.5, which came from the same type of supernova and looks very similar. Claude Cornen's version of this image won sixth prize in the Hubble's Hidden Treasures competition.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged the remnant through a visual filter and a filter near the hydrogen-alpha line. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The thin shells glow faintly in hydrogen light and would be invisible to the eye at this distance.

alt: Thin, delicate red shells of gas from an exploded star.

caption: The nebula Sh2-46 (Gum 80) and the star HD 165319, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: Strong red clouds surround a big blue-white star at the centre of this picture. The cloud is the nebula Sh2-46, also named Gum 80, and the star is HD 165319. It seems to belong there, but astronomers think it is an impostor.

HD 165319 is an O-type star, among the brightest but rarest kinds of star. Its radiation ionises the hydrogen in the nebula, producing much of the red glow. Astronomers think, however, that it was born elsewhere, in the nearby Eagle Nebula, a busy star-forming region. Stars born together usually stay bound in an open cluster, but a few break free and wander, sometimes into unrelated nebulae.

A curved shock front beside the star, like the wave in front of a moving boat, suggests the star is currently plunging through Sh2-46. If the star eventually moves on, the nebula may end up looking quite different.
explore: The VLT Survey Telescope, owned by the Italian National Institute for Astrophysics (INAF) and located at ESO's Paranal Observatory, took this detailed visible-light picture. It marked a centenary, the 100 years of the Planetarium, and a full-dome version was screened at the ESO Supernova Planetarium & Visitor Centre.

understand.summary: The VLT Survey Telescope took this image in visible light. The filters and colour mapping aren't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures gather far more light than the eye, making the red glow much stronger than it would appear directly.

scaleExtra: The nebula is roughly 6000 light-years away, according to ESO.
alt: Strong red clouds of gas surrounding a big blue-white star at the centre.

caption: The supernova remnant SNR 0509-67.5, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Two concentric shells of blue sit inside a glow of orange in this image of SNR 0509-67.5. This spreading debris is all that is left of a star which blew up several centuries ago.

The colours are a chemical map. The data come from MUSE, the Multi-Unit Spectroscopic Explorer on ESO's Very Large Telescope, which can show where each chemical element lies. Calcium is shown in blue and hydrogen in orange.

The two calcium shells are the key finding. They indicate that the star died in a double detonation, exploding with two blasts rather than one. According to ESO, this is the first photographic evidence that stars can die this way. The two nested layers of calcium are read as the signature of those two blasts, preserved in the debris of the star as it spreads.
explore: The background stars in the image come from Hubble data, while the chemical map of the remnant comes from the VLT. MUSE records a spectrum at every point, which is what allows each element to be pulled out and coloured separately.

understand.summary: The VLT's MUSE instrument mapped individual elements in visible light. Calcium is shown in blue and hydrogen (H-alpha) in orange, with background stars from Hubble.
understand.eye: MUSE separates the light of individual elements, something no eye can do, so this is a map of chemistry rather than a direct view.

alt: Two concentric blue shells inside an orange glow, surrounded by stars.

caption: The IC4701 nebula, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: Intense reddish gas and dark clouds of dust mingle with a crowd of stars in this view of the IC4701 nebula in the constellation Sagittarius. On the sky, the nebula spans twice the width of the full Moon.

The red colour comes from hydrogen. Energetic light from newborn stars ionises the gas, and it responds by shining in that particular reddish hue. The dark clouds are rich in interstellar dust, so thick that light from the stars behind them cannot get through.

IC4701 is part of a vast complex of dust and gas where new stars are springing to life. Most stars are born cooler, redder and less massive than the Sun. Hot, massive stars are much rarer and burn through their fuel quickly before dying. That short life makes brilliant blue massive stars, and the glowing gas around them, signposts of recent star formation.
explore: The image was taken with OmegaCAM, the wide-field camera on the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory, and the data come from the VPHAS+ survey.

understand.summary: The VLT Survey Telescope's OmegaCAM camera recorded this visible-light image through u, g, r and i filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The hydrogen filter and long exposures reveal a red glow far too faint to see with the eye.

alt: Reddish glowing gas and dark dust clouds among many stars.

caption: The planetary nebula NGC 2371, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Prominent pink clouds lie on opposite sides of a central star in this glowing bubble of gas, with many tiny pink dots also lined up across the star. This is NGC 2371 in Gemini, a planetary nebula made from the cast-off gas of a star much like the Sun.

The star at the centre is the super-hot core of a former red giant, stripped of its outer layers, with a surface temperature of about 240,000 degrees Fahrenheit. Its ultraviolet light makes the nebula glow. The pink colour shows the paired clouds are relatively cool and dense.

The small pink knots seem to mark gas thrown out in a specific direction, and that direction has shifted over the past few thousand years. The reason is not well understood, though a second star orbiting the central one might be responsible. Within a few thousand years the nebula will fade away, and the star will cool into a white dwarf.
explore: NGC 2371 lies about 4,300 light-years away. The images were taken with Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 as part of the Hubble Heritage programme, and they revealed many structures not seen before.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 made this false-colour image. Filters for sulfur and nitrogen are shown in red, hydrogen in green and oxygen in blue.
understand.eye: It is a false-colour image in which each gas is assigned its own colour, so it does not show what an eye would see.

caption: The frEGG J025157.5+600606, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A dark, compact globule of dust and gas is outlined by glowing purple and blue edges in this Hubble image. It is a free-floating evaporating gaseous globule, or frEGG, a special kind of star-forming nursery, formally known as J025157.5+600606.

FrEGGs live in harsh surroundings. When a massive new star begins to shine while still inside the cool molecular cloud that formed it, its energetic radiation ionises the cloud's hydrogen and blows a large, hot bubble of ionised gas. Surprisingly, dark frEGGs survive inside such bubbles around nearby massive stars, and some of them are giving birth to low-mass stars.

The glowing edge marks the boundary where the cool, dusty globule meets the hot gas around it. There, radiation from the massive star is slowly eating away at the globule, which is why it is described as evaporating.
explore: An earlier ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week, in July 2020, featured another of these globules, catalogued as J025027.7+600849.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged the globule through visible and near-infrared filters and a filter for nitrogen emission. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The glowing rim is faint and partly recorded in light the eye cannot see, so it would not be visible directly.

alt: A dark compact globule of dust and gas with glowing purple and blue edges.

caption: The star-forming region NGC 6559, imaged by the Danish 1.54-metre telescope at La Silla
story: Red clouds, blue patches and dark regions jostle together in this image of NGC 6559, a place where stars are forming inside an interstellar cloud. It was taken with the Danish 1.54-metre telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile.

Each colour tells of a different process. The red clouds are made mostly of hydrogen gas, which glows when it is energised. The blue areas are where starlight bounces off tiny particles of dust, much as sunlight scatters in Earth's sky. The dark regions are places where dust is so thick that it becomes opaque and blocks the light behind it.
ESO describes the scene as showing the anarchy that reigns when stars form, with glowing gas, reflecting dust and dark clouds tangled together in one patch of sky.

understand.summary: The DFOSC instrument on the Danish 1.54-metre telescope took this visible-light image through B, V, R and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The camera's long exposures reveal faint coloured clouds that the eye could not see.

alt: Red glowing gas clouds, blue reflection patches and dark opaque dust regions among stars.

caption: The Gum 41 nebula, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: A rosy, fairly symmetric shell of glowing hydrogen stands out against a colourful backdrop of stars. This is the Gum 41 nebula in the southern constellation of Centaurus.

Gum 41 is a Strömgren sphere, a shell of hydrogen made to glow by radiation from a bright central star. That star, HD 100099, looks like one object, but it is thought to be two young, massive stars orbiting so closely that they cannot be told apart here. The region holds many such pairs, including HD 99944, the bright object on the lower right edge.

These partnerships will not last. Hot, massive stars have short lives of only a few million years, unlike our Sun. Once they are gone, nothing will be left to make the nebula glow, and Gum 41 will fade into transparency.
explore: Gum 41 belongs to a much larger region nicknamed the Running Chicken Nebula. Whether Gum 41 is the chicken's foot or its head is, according to ESO, surprisingly controversial. The picture was taken with the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory.

understand.summary: The VLT Survey Telescope took this visible-light image. The filters and colour mapping aren't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures bring out the rosy hydrogen glow, which would be far fainter to the eye.

alt: A rosy, symmetric shell of glowing gas around a bright central star, against a colourful star field.

caption: The nebulae Gum 10 and Gum 11, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: Red-orange clouds sprawl across this picture, streaked with black lines. The bright cloud that dominates is Gum 10, and the fainter, separate cloud at the bottom left is Gum 11. Some viewers may see a chicken pecking at seeds, or the head of a dragon.

The pair belong to a larger complex where stars are born, visible mostly from the southern hemisphere. Hot, massive stars in each nebula give off ultraviolet light strong enough to tear electrons away from hydrogen atoms. When the electrons later rejoin the hydrogen ions, they give off the particular shade of red. The black lines are dust blocking the light behind it.

The picture was released on the fifteenth anniversary of first light for the VLT Survey Telescope, which took it. The data come from VPHAS+, a project scanning the plane of the Milky Way to better understand the life cycle of stars.
explore: The VST began as a joint project between ESO and the Capodimonte Astronomical Observatory, which belongs to INAF, Italy's national astrophysics institute. Today INAF manages it alone, and ESO hosts it at Paranal Observatory in Chile.

understand.summary: The VLT Survey Telescope took this visible-light image. The filters and colour mapping aren't published.
understand.eye: The camera builds up a red glow from hydrogen over long exposures, far brighter than the eye would see it.

alt: Large red-orange clouds with black dust lanes, and a smaller detached cloud at bottom left.

caption: The molecular cloud IRAS 16562-3959, imaged by ESO's VISTA telescope
story: An orange smudge sits among a rich pool of stars at the centre of this infrared view. It is a dense cloud of dust and gas linked to the molecular cloud IRAS 16562-3959, in the constellation Scorpius close to the central plane of our galaxy.

Clouds like this are breeding grounds for stars. At its centre, a bright object called G345.4938+01.4677 can just be seen through the veil of gas and dust. It is a very young star, still forming as the cloud collapses under gravity, and it is heavy, at roughly 15 times the Sun's mass.

Observations with ALMA, a radio telescope array, found something unexpected around it, a large disc of gas and dust and a stream of material flowing out. Theory predicted neither should exist, because strong radiation from such massive newborn stars is expected to push material away.
explore: The image comes from VISTA at ESO's Paranal Observatory, the world's largest survey telescope, with a main mirror over four metres across. It was produced by the VVV survey, one of six large public surveys mapping the southern sky. The bright star at bottom left is HD 153220.

understand.summary: VISTA's VIRCAM camera imaged this region in near-infrared light through J, H and Ks filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and it lets the camera see partly through dust that would hide the young star.

alt: An orange smudge of dust and gas among a dense field of stars, with a bright star at bottom left.

caption: The red supergiant Stephenson 2 DFK 52 and its cloud of ejected material, imaged by ALMA
story: Blue and red overlap in this image, rather like an old 3D picture meant for paper red-and-cyan glasses. It actually shows a red supergiant star, Stephenson 2 DFK 52, which is shedding gas and dust into space as its life draws to a close.

Such clouds are common around supergiants, but this one is a puzzle. It is the largest cloud of ejected material yet found around a supergiant. Astronomers expected something like the cloud around Betelgeuse, a similar star. Instead, if DFK 52 were as close as Betelgeuse, its cocoon would look a third as wide as the full Moon.

The colours show motion, with blue for gas moving toward us and red for gas moving away. The data suggest that about 4000 years ago the star shed mass at an extreme rate, before slowing to a pace more like Betelgeuse's. How it lost so much so quickly is still a mystery.
explore: DFK 52 is estimated to be 10-15 times as massive as the Sun and has already lost 5-10% of its mass. Astronomers ask whether a companion star was involved, why the cloud's shape is so complex, and whether similar supergiants exist. The star is expected to explode as a supernova sometime in the next million years.

understand.summary: The Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) observed the star at millimetre wavelengths, tracing carbon monoxide gas and dust. Blue marks gas moving towards us and red gas moving away.
understand.eye: Millimetre-wavelength radio light is invisible to the eye, and the colours encode motion rather than any colour the gas really has.

scaleExtra: The cloud of ejected material is about 1.4 light-years across, according to ESO.
alt: An overlapping blue and red cloud of gas surrounding a red supergiant star, resembling a 3D image.

caption: The supernova remnant N 49 (DEM L 190), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Delicate filaments spread across this Hubble image like puffs of smoke and sparks from a fireworks display. They are really sheets of debris from a stellar explosion in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small companion galaxy of the Milky Way that can be seen from the southern hemisphere.

The remnant is called N 49, or DEM L 190. A massive star made it when it perished in a supernova, and the light of that blast would have reached Earth thousands of years ago. The remnant lies about 170,000 light-years away.

This wreckage will not go to waste. The filaments will eventually be recycled into new generations of stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud. The same thing happened in our own galaxy, where the Sun and its planets were built from similar debris, left by stars in the Milky Way that blew up billions of years ago.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 took this image through filters for oxygen, hydrogen-alpha and sulphur emission plus yellow and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Filters that isolate glowing gases, and near-infrared light we cannot see, reveal filaments far too faint for the eye.

alt: Delicate filaments of glowing debris resembling smoke and sparks from fireworks.

caption: The planetary nebula NGC 2899, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: This highly detailed picture shows NGC 2899, a planetary nebula in the constellation Vela. Even its faint outer edges glow over the background stars, and according to ESO the object had never before been imaged in such detail. It was captured with the FORS instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope in northern Chile.

A planetary nebula is the cloud of gas thrown off by a Sun-like star near the end of its life. As the star's outer layers drift away, its exposed hot core sends out ultraviolet light that makes the gas glow. Despite the name, these objects have nothing to do with planets.

The FORS instrument brought out the nebula's structure in fine detail, from its bright inner parts to the faint glow at its outer edges. The image combines several filters, including one tuned to the light of glowing oxygen.

understand.summary: The VLT's FORS2 instrument took this visible-light image through b, v and R filters plus an oxygen filter. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The faint outer edges only show up in the telescope's long exposures. To the eye they would be invisible.

alt: A detailed planetary nebula whose faint outer edges glow over background stars.

caption: The nebula Gum 39 in the Running Chicken Nebula, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: A pink glow of hydrogen gas, crossed by dark lanes of dust, is surrounded by orange, white and blue stars scattered like fireworks. This is Gum 39, a nebula in the constellation Centaurus.

The much larger Running Chicken Nebula was captured in a 1.5-billion-pixel image, and Gum 39 is only a small piece of it. It forms the comb on the chicken's head, at least in some people's eyes, since viewers disagree about what the chicken looks like. The data were captured by the VLT Survey Telescope, which belongs to Italy's national astrophysics institute and is hosted and run by ESO.

The pink glow comes from hydrogen lit up by intense radiation from newborn stars, and the dark lanes are dust blocking the light behind them. Nebulae like this are called stellar nurseries, because as dense clouds of molecular gas collapse under gravity, they give rise to many new stars.
explore: Scientists use telescopes such as the VST and ALMA to study these nurseries and better understand the complex process of star birth. Gum 39 is the object's official name.

understand.summary: The VLT Survey Telescope took this visible-light image. The filters and colour mapping aren't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures bring out a pink glow and faint stars that the eye could not see.

scaleExtra: Gum 39 is about 6500 light-years from Earth, according to ESO.
alt: Pink glowing gas crossed by dark dust lanes, surrounded by orange, white and blue stars.

caption: The Skull Nebula (NGC 246), imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Pink and red tones fill this detailed view of the Skull Nebula, also known as NGC 246, in the constellation Cetus. It was captured by ESO's Very Large Telescope using its FORS instrument.

The Skull Nebula is a planetary nebula, a shell of gas cast off by a dying Sun-like star. As the star loses its outer layers, its hot exposed core lights up the surrounding gas with ultraviolet radiation, making it glow.

What makes NGC 246 special is the family at its heart. It is the first planetary nebula found to be linked with a pair of closely bound stars that are orbited by a third, more distant star. The picture combines several filters, including ones that pick out glowing oxygen and hydrogen.

understand.summary: The VLT's FORS2 instrument captured this visible-light image through b, v and R filters plus oxygen and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The telescope's exposures and gas filters bring out glowing structure that would be very faint to the eye.

alt: A planetary nebula glowing in pink and red tones.

caption: The Southern Ring Nebula (NGC 3132), imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A large, translucent pink-and-red oval, slightly misshapen and tilted from top left to bottom right, surrounds a single visible star at the centre. This is the Southern Ring Nebula, NGC 3132, seen by Webb's Near-Infrared Camera and Mid-Infrared Instrument together.
The nebula is made of gas cast off by the star at its centre. Webb's image traces the star's scattered outflows that have reached farther out into space.

Outside a band of cooler gas, most of the molecular gas is also cold, but it is far clumpier. It gathers into dense knots of molecular gas, which together form a halo around the central stars. The three filters used record molecular hydrogen at two wavelengths and PAH emission at a third. The nebula is about 2,500 light-years away.

understand.summary: This composite combines Webb's NIRCam and MIRI data from three filters. Molecular hydrogen at 2.12 microns is shown in blue, molecular hydrogen at 4.7 microns in green and PAH emission at 7.7 microns in red.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye, so the colours are assigned to show different kinds of material.

alt: A translucent pink-and-red misshapen oval nebula around a single central star, tilted from top left to bottom right.

caption: The gas cloud IC 2948 in the Running Chicken Nebula, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: Countless young stars are scattered through this gas cloud, and creeping dark clouds shaped like open hands seem ready to grab them. This is IC2948, the brightest region of the Running Chicken Nebula in the constellation Centaurus.

The Running Chicken Nebula is enormous, covering an area of sky close to 25 full moons. The view shown here covers less than a third of one full moon. Such a detailed close-up came from a 1.5-billion-pixel image made by the VLT Survey Telescope, hosted and operated by ESO.

The nebula is a maze of gas and dust, and the intense radiation of its young stars wears away the material around them. IC2948 was first discovered more than a century ago, and it is still helping astronomers understand how stars form and behave in their infancy.
explore: To find IC2948 in the larger nebula, look for the chicken's rear end, though others say that spot is the head. Nearby you may also spot other regions, such as the Gum 41 nebula.

understand.summary: The VLT Survey Telescope took this visible-light image. The filters and colour mapping aren't published.
understand.eye: The long exposures reveal glowing gas and faint stars well beyond what an eye could see.

alt: A glowing gas cloud crowded with young stars and dark, hand-shaped clouds.

caption: The Retina Nebula (IC 4406), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A rainbow of colours and fine tendrils fill this Hubble view of IC 4406, a dying star's nebula whose left and right halves are nearly mirror images. That symmetry is common among planetary nebulae, the clouds of gas cast off by stars near the end of their lives.

Its true shape is hidden by our viewpoint. If we could fly around IC 4406, we would see the gas and dust form a vast doughnut streaming outward from the dying star. From Hubble, near Earth, we see that doughnut from the side, so its ring shape does not show.

The side-on view also reveals intricate tendrils of material that have been likened to the retina at the back of an eye. That comparison gave IC 4406 its nickname, the Retina Nebula. The nebula lies about 5,000 light-years away in the constellation Lupus.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 imaged the nebula through filters for oxygen, hydrogen-alpha and nitrogen emission. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Filters that isolate individual glowing gases produce colour distinctions the eye could not see.

alt: A symmetric nebula in a rainbow of colours with intricate tendrils resembling a retina.

caption: The planetary nebula Abell 24, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: A faint, red-hued cloud of gas glows in this image. It is Abell 24, a planetary nebula in Canis Minor, the Lesser Dog, made of gas and dust thrown into space when a star dies. The name is misleading. William Herschel, who also discovered Uranus, coined it because such fuzzy objects looked like giant planets in early telescopes.

A Sun-like star spends most of its life turning hydrogen into helium in its core. When the fuel runs out, the core collapses and heats up while the outer layers swell, and the star becomes a red giant. When the Sun does this it will engulf the innermost planets and possibly Earth, swelling until its radius is more than 250 times what it is today.

Strong winds then blow off the outer layers, which spread into space. That exposes the hot core, whose ultraviolet light makes the gas glow. Abell 24 is that faint glow around the bright remnant of a long-dead star.
explore: The image was taken with the VLT's FORS instrument as part of ESO's Cosmic Gems programme, which uses telescope time that cannot be used for science to make outreach images. The data are also archived for astronomers.

understand.summary: The VLT's FORS2 instrument captured this visible-light image through b, V, R and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The nebula's glow is faint, and the camera's exposures record far more of it than the eye could.

alt: A faint red cloud of gas around a bright central star.

caption: Two merging star clusters in the 30 Doradus Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Two star clusters fill this Hubble image, and astronomers think they have just begun to merge. They lie in the gigantic 30 Doradus Nebula, also known as the Tarantula, 170,000 light-years from Earth.

The evidence for the coming collision is circumstantial. The cluster at upper left looks stretched out, and the two clusters appear to have different ages. A merger would also explain the puzzlingly large number of fast-moving stars around 30 Doradus. They could be accounted for if a small cluster has merged into R136, the big cluster at the centre of the nebula.
Because the two clusters are close by, astronomers can study their interaction in detail, and it may shed light on how clusters of stars might have formed in the early Universe.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 made this image in ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light. Blue shows light from the hottest, most massive stars, green the glow of oxygen, and red fluorescing hydrogen.
understand.eye: Part of the data is ultraviolet and near-infrared light that the eye cannot see, and gas-specific filters separate oxygen from hydrogen.

alt: Two star clusters in a glowing nebula, one of them elongated, with blue stars and green and red gas.

caption: Dense star-forming gas in the RCW 106 region, imaged by APEX and the VLT Survey Telescope
story: Glowing red clouds lie over a field of stars in this picture of the RCW 106 region. The red marks dense gas where new stars are being born. It is a map made with the ArTéMiS camera on the Atacama Pathfinder Experiment (APEX), laid over an optical image from the VLT Survey Telescope.

The region points to a puzzle. Only about 1% of this gas will ever become stars, and astronomers don't know why the share is so low. Stars form when parts of huge clouds of cold gas clump together and collapse, which happens once the gas reaches a critical density.

Even denser regions might be expected to make even more stars, but new APEX results suggest that packing gas more tightly does not make a region better at turning it into stars. One possible reason is the way these dense clouds break up into filaments and cores, the seeds of future stars. Many questions remain open.
explore: The APEX results were accepted for publication in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics. APEX is continuing to investigate why so little gas turns into stars, and the highlighted red regions show the areas of interest for that work.

understand.summary: This composite overlays a red map of dense gas from the ArTéMiS camera on APEX, which observes at submillimetre wavelengths, onto an optical image from the VLT Survey Telescope.
understand.eye: The red layer shows submillimetre light from cold dense gas, which the eye cannot see at all. Only the background comes from visible light.

alt: Glowing red regions of dense gas overlaid on a starry optical image.
flags: overlay: APEX submillimetre dense-gas map laid over an optical VST image

caption: The nebula IRAS 05437+2502, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A little-known nebula billows out among bright stars and dark dust clouds in this Hubble image, with a bright, sharp-edged boomerang-shaped arc standing out. The nebula is IRAS 05437+2502, in Taurus, the Bull, near the central plane of the Milky Way.

Few detailed studies of it exist, unlike many objects Hubble looks at, so what it really is remains uncertain. On first inspection it seems to be a small, fairly isolated star-forming region, shaped by ultraviolet light from young stars.

The boomerang arc may tell a different story. It could have been created by a fast young star ploughing through the cloud of gas and dust. Such a star would have been thrown out of the distant young cluster where it formed, and would be racing through the nebula at 200 000 km/hour or more.
explore: The Infrared Astronomical Satellite, IRAS, found this cloud in 1983. IRAS was the first space telescope to map the entire sky in infrared. Hubble took this picture as part of a snapshot survey, filling gaps in its schedule with no guarantee the observation would happen at all.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys combined yellow (F606W) and near-infrared (F814W) filters, with about eleven minutes per filter. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and eleven-minute exposures reveal faint gas well beyond naked-eye reach.

alt: A billowing nebula among bright stars and dark dust, with a bright sharp-edged boomerang-shaped arc.

caption: The planetary nebula NGC 2392, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This is NGC 2392, a planetary nebula in the constellation Gemini, made of the glowing remains of a dying star much like the Sun. It was among the first views Hubble captured after the successful servicing mission of December 1999.

A planetary nebula forms when a Sun-like star reaches the end of its life. The star puffs off its outer layers of gas, which drift out into space. The exposed hot core left behind shines with strong ultraviolet light, and that light makes the surrounding gas glow. The name comes from early astronomers, who thought such round fuzzy objects looked a little like planets, but they have nothing to do with planets.

Servicing missions sent astronauts to repair and upgrade Hubble in orbit, and this image came from the telescope's first look at the sky after the one in December 1999. It used filters that pick out the glow of helium, oxygen, hydrogen and nitrogen.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 imaged the nebula through filters for helium, oxygen, hydrogen-alpha and nitrogen emission. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Filters that isolate individual gases give each one a colour, which is not how an eye would see the nebula.

alt: A glowing planetary nebula around a dying star.

caption: The Boomerang Nebula, imaged by ALMA and the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A purple double-lobed shape with a very narrow waist sits behind a more elongated orange shape in this view of the Boomerang Nebula. The purple is Hubble's visible-light view, and the orange is cold molecular gas seen by ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, revealing the nebula's longer true shape.

The Boomerang is a protoplanetary nebula, about 5,000 light-years away, and since 2003 it has held the record as the coldest known object in the Universe. Astronomers think it grew out of the outer envelope of an ageing star after that star engulfed a smaller companion. That may explain its ultra-cold outflows, which are lit by the dying central star.

ALMA examined the dusty central disc and the outflows further out. Those outflows are colder even than the cosmic microwave background, the faint afterglow of the Big Bang, and they are expanding at 590 000 kilometres per hour.
explore: The outflows stretch almost four light-years across the sky, and reach temperatures below -270 °C. The combined picture shows how different the same object can look depending on the kind of light used to observe it.

understand.summary: This combines ALMA observations of carbon monoxide gas at submillimetre wavelengths (orange) with a visible-light Hubble image (purple).
understand.eye: The orange ALMA data trace submillimetre light from cold gas, which is invisible to the eye.

alt: A purple double-lobed nebula with a narrow centre, overlaid with a longer orange shape of cold gas.

caption: The wind nebula M1-67 around the star WR124, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: This image shows M1-67, a nebula blown by the wind of a star called WR124. It is the youngest known wind nebula around a Wolf-Rayet star in our galaxy, and it lies about 10,000 light-years away.

Wolf-Rayet stars begin life with dozens of times the Sun's mass, but they lose most of it through a powerful wind. That wind is what ultimately builds nebulae like M1-67. Eventually WR124 will explode as a supernova, blowing everything around it away.

Earlier Hubble observations had shown that the nebula is full of little knots and fine structure. That team, led by Cédric Foellmi of ESO, returned with ESO's Very Large Telescope to see how those structures have changed. Watching them evolve can reveal how stellar winds behave, what they are made of, and how they blend into the gas and dust between the stars.
explore: The image uses FORS1 data taken by the Paranal Science team through 2 wide filters (B and V) and 3 narrow-band filters. The broad filters capture overall colour, while the narrow ones isolate light from specific glowing gases in the wind.

understand.summary: The VLT's FORS1 instrument took this visible-light image through two broadband filters (B and V) and three narrow-band filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The narrow-band filters isolate specific glowing gases, showing structure an eye could not pick out.

alt: The wind nebula M1-67 around the Wolf-Rayet star WR124.

caption: The supernova remnant Cassiopeia A, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Glowing streamers of red, white and blue, with touches of green and pink, float across this Hubble photo like festive fireworks. They were made by a huge supernova explosion, the death of a massive star.

The shredded remains are called Cassiopeia A, or Cas A. No younger supernova remnant is known in our Milky Way galaxy. Cas A sits in the constellation Cassiopeia. Light from the explosion reached Earth about 320 years ago, in the late 1600s.

The remnant is so far away that the star actually exploded long before anyone could see it, since its light had to travel across the whole distance to reach us. The colourful streamers Hubble recorded are the shredded remains of that star, still glowing in many colours.
explore: Cas A lies about ten thousand light-years away, which means the star blew up that many years before its light arrived here in the late 1600s.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 imaged the remnant through blue, red and near-infrared filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, invisible to us, and the streamers are much too faint for the eye to see.

alt: Glowing gaseous streamers in red, white, blue, green and pink spreading across the sky.
flags: distance mismatch: caption says 10,000 light-years, metadata 11000

caption: The young star Ve 7-27 and the Vela Junior supernova remnant, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Energetic jets studded with knots, like bullets, shoot out of one object in this picture, while a compact yellowish-green smudge sits centre-left. The object with jets is Ve 7-27, which astronomers long believed was a planetary nebula, the final stage in the life of a star like the Sun. ESO's Very Large Telescope has shown it is actually a baby star still forming.

MUSE, an instrument on the VLT, captured the first detailed image of it. Jets with knots are typical of newborn stars. Lead author Janette Suherli described it as a newborn rather than a dying star's last breath.

A dead star is nearby too. The yellowish-green smudge hosts a neutron star left by a supernova, part of the Vela Junior remnant. The baby star is embedded in that supernova's debris, so the two are at the same distance. That finally pins down the remnant's size, expansion speed, energy and age.
explore: Suherli is a PhD candidate at the University of Manitoba in Canada. She describes the scene as a star being born right beside the remains of one that died, and the finding resolves decades of inconsistencies about Vela Junior.

understand.summary: The VLT's MUSE instrument imaged the region in visible light, using the emission of nickel, nitrogen and hydrogen-alpha. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: MUSE separates the light of individual elements, revealing jets and knots the eye could not distinguish.

scaleExtra: Ve 7-27, and therefore Vela Junior, is about 4500 light-years away, according to ESO.
alt: A young star shooting knotty jets, with a compact yellowish-green smudge to the centre-left.

caption: The Twin Jet Nebula (M2-9), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows M2-9, a bipolar planetary nebula, also described as a butterfly. A more revealing name might be the Twin Jet Nebula, because if you imagine slicing across the star, each side looks like a pair of exhausts from a jet engine.

That comparison is more than a figure of speech. The nebula's shape, and the speed of its gas, which moves at more than 200 miles per second, lead astronomers to describe it as a super-supersonic jet exhaust. The gas is streaming out from a central star in two opposite directions.

Ground-based studies have measured the nebula growing over time. Working backwards from that expansion suggests that the outburst which formed the lobes happened only about twelve centuries ago, which is very recent by astronomical standards. Planetary nebulae form when dying Sun-like stars shed their outer layers, and M2-9's lobes show how violent that shedding can be. The nebula lies about 2,000 light-years away.
explore: The gas speed of more than 200 miles per second is roughly 322 kilometres per second. M2-9 is a clear example of the butterfly, or bipolar, type of planetary nebula.

understand.summary: The Hubble instrument, filters and colour mapping used for this image aren't published.
understand.eye: The nebula's faint lobes are far beyond what the eye could see without a large telescope and long exposures.

alt: A bipolar planetary nebula with two lobes extending in opposite directions like jet exhausts.

caption: Part of the emission nebula NGC 6357, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: A mesh of red-glowing gas, dark dust and newly born and still-forming stars fills this close-up. The area is a small part of NGC 6357, a well-known emission nebula in the tail of Scorpius, the Scorpion. It was captured by ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal.

The red is typical of an H II region, a cloud rich in ionised and excited hydrogen. The cloud is flooded with intense ultraviolet light, coming mostly from Pismis 24, an open cluster that contains several massive, young blue stars. The gas absorbs that radiation and gives it back as visible light in this distinctive red.

The cluster itself sits out of view. Its diffuse light can be seen brightening the cloud on the centre-right. What remains in view is the surrounding nebula, where the next generation of stars is taking shape amid the gas and dust.
explore: NGC 6357 lies some 8000 light-years away. Pismis 24's massive blue stars are the main source of the ultraviolet light that powers the glow across this part of the nebula.

understand.summary: The Very Large Telescope took this visible-light image. The instrument, filters and colour mapping aren't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal the red glow and faint stars far more strongly than the eye could see them.

alt: A mesh of red glowing gas and dark dust with young stars, brighter at centre-right.

caption: The emission nebula Sh 2-305, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: A gently glowing patch of sky fills this image. It is in fact Sh 2-305, a hot bubble of hydrogen gas lit up by intense radiation from nearby stars. Clouds like this are called emission nebulae, or HII regions, pronounced H-two.

The ultraviolet light behind the glow is thought to come from at least two O-type stars, and probably several others. O-type stars are the brightest and hottest kind known. They can hold up to 90 times the Sun's mass and shine one million times as brightly. Their radiation strips electrons from the hydrogen, which then glows.

Sh 2-305 is part of something much bigger. With five neighbouring bubbles, it belongs to a giant complex of dense dust and gas clouds, and on a larger scale to an enormous ring called the GS234-02 star-forming supershell. The supershell sits in the Milky Way's Perseus arm, toward the constellation Puppis.
explore: The picture was taken through the ESO Cosmic Gems programme, which turns telescope time unsuitable for science into outreach images, using the FORS instrument on the Very Large Telescope. The data also go into ESO's science archive for astronomers.

understand.summary: The VLT's FORS2 instrument took this visible-light image through B, V, R and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The glow is faint, and the hydrogen filter and long exposures make it far more visible than it would be to the eye.

alt: A gently glowing bubble of hydrogen gas scattered with stars.

caption: Part of the Gum 10 nebula, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: A sea of scarlet gas, broken by dark patches, fills this view of part of the Gum 10 nebula in the constellation Puppis, seen through ESO's Very Large Telescope in Chile.

The colour has a clear cause. Hot blue stars inside Gum 10 pour out energetic ultraviolet radiation that ionises the nebula's gas, stripping electrons from their atoms. When the electrons rejoin the atoms, they give off light at very particular colours. In Gum 10 the red is the signature of hydrogen, which is more plentiful than any other element in the Universe.

Darker patches mark thick clouds of dust that partly block our view of whatever lies behind them. The nebula takes its name from the Australian astronomer Colin Stanley Gum, who discovered it and in 1955 published a catalogue of more than 80 similar diffuse nebulae.
explore: The image was taken with the FORS2 instrument as part of ESO's Cosmic Gems programme, which uses telescope time that cannot be used for science to make outreach images. The data are also made available to astronomers through ESO's science archive.

understand.summary: The VLT's FORS2 instrument took this visible-light image through b, v and R filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The hydrogen filter and long exposures bring out a red glow that would be very faint to the eye.

alt: Scarlet glowing gas with dark patches of dust and scattered stars.

caption: Kepler's Supernova remnant, imaged by the Chandra X-ray Observatory
story: This image shows the remains of Kepler's Supernova, seen by NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory. It is the most recent exploding star to have been seen in our Milky Way galaxy.

When people first saw it, 400 years ago, they thought a new star had appeared. In reality, it was a star blowing itself apart, its gas and dust rushing outward. That debris is still spreading today, racing outward at 4 million miles per hour, and it has now grown to 14 light-years across.

X-ray telescopes are well suited to remnants like this. The blast wave from a supernova heats gas to extremely high temperatures, hot enough to shine brightly in X-rays. Chandra can map that hot gas. Because X-rays are absorbed by Earth's atmosphere, such observations must be made from space. The remnant lies about 13,000 light-years away in the constellation Ophiuchus.

understand.summary: This is an X-ray image from the Chandra X-ray Observatory. How X-ray energies were mapped to colours isn't published.
understand.eye: X-rays are invisible to the human eye, so any colours here are a translation of light we cannot see.

caption: The supernova remnant NGC 2060, imaged by ESO
story: This picture shows NGC 2060, the aftermath of a supernova in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy near our own, about 170,000 light-years away. On our sky it lies in the direction of the constellation Dorado.
A supernova marks the violent death of a massive star. The explosion blasts heated matter out into the surrounding space at great speed, and what is left behind is called a supernova remnant.

ESO describes the remnant NGC 2060 as resplendent. Its host, the Large Magellanic Cloud, is a small companion of the Milky Way that appears in the direction of Dorado on our sky, so the remnant is the wreckage of a massive star in another galaxy rather than in our own.

understand.summary: The telescope, instrument, filters and colour mapping for this ESO image aren't published.
understand.eye: The remnant is far too faint and distant to see with the eye. A telescope's long exposure is needed.

alt: The glowing aftermath of a supernova in a neighbouring galaxy.

caption: The HII region DG121, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: A soft purple haze with no sharp edges spreads across this picture, with a bright star near the centre. This is DG121, a glowing cloud of ionised hydrogen known as an HII region, in the constellation Puppis, the Stern.

HII regions are a kind of emission nebula. They form when young, massive stars give off enough ultraviolet energy to ionise the gas clouds around them, making the gas glow. Their structure tends to be irregular, without crisp boundaries, which gives them their hazy but photogenic look. The brightest star in the region, near the centre, is HD 60068.

The image was taken with FORS2 on ESO's Very Large Telescope in the Chilean Atacama Desert. Astronomers have nicknamed it Paranal's Swiss army knife, because it can study many kinds of objects in many different ways. In this case it worked as a camera, recording the nebula through several colour filters.
explore: FORS2 stands for FOcal Reducer and low dispersion Spectrograph 2. Besides taking images, it can spread light into spectra, which lets astronomers measure what objects are made of and how they move.

understand.summary: The VLT's FORS2 instrument took this visible-light image through B, V, R and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The haze is faint, and the camera's long exposures make it far more visible than it would appear to the eye.

alt: A soft purple haze of glowing gas with a bright star near the centre.

caption: The Flame Nebula (NGC 2024), imaged by the Danish 1.54-metre telescope at La Silla
story: On the fringe of a huge cloud of gas and dust shines the Flame Nebula, with a dark, forked structure of dust across the centre of the image. The nebula, also known as NGC 2024, lies towards the constellation of Orion.
In fact it conceals a cluster of massive, young, blue stars. Their light sets the gas ablaze, and the nebula's typical colour comes from hydrogen atoms heated by these stars.

The stars themselves stay out of sight. They are hidden behind that dark, forked band of dust, and only infrared observations can reveal them, because infrared light passes through dust far more easily than visible light. This visible-light picture shows the glowing gas the stars light up rather than the stars. It was built from three short exposures with the 1.5-metre Danish telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile, through blue, visual and red filters.
explore: The exposures lasted 40 seconds in B, 80 seconds in V and 40 seconds in R. The Flame Nebula lies about 1,300 light-years away.

understand.summary: The DFOSC camera on the Danish 1.54-metre telescope took this visible-light image through B, V and R filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Even with telescope exposures, visible light can't reach the hidden stars. Seeing them takes infrared, which the eye cannot detect.

caption: The Little Ghost Nebula (NGC 6369), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A colourful cloud surrounds a faint central star in this Hubble view. It is NGC 6369, the glowing remains of a dying star, which amateur astronomers know as the Little Ghost Nebula because it appears as a small, ghostly cloud around its faint central star.

NGC 6369 is a planetary nebula. When a star like the Sun nears the end of its life, it throws off its outer layers of gas. The hot core that remains gives off strong ultraviolet light, which makes the expelled gas glow. Despite the name, these objects are unrelated to planets.

Hubble's image combines several filters, some tuned to the light of particular gases such as oxygen, hydrogen and nitrogen. The nebula lies about 3,500 light-years away in the constellation Ophiuchus.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 imaged the nebula through broadband and near-infrared filters and filters for oxygen, hydrogen-alpha and nitrogen emission. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Hubble's filters, including near-infrared light we cannot see, reveal colour and detail the eye cannot.

caption: The Orion Nebula and Trapezium cluster, imaged by the Danish 1.54-metre telescope at La Silla
story: Clouds of glowing gas in many colours and shapes spread across this picture of the Orion Nebula, also known as Messier 42. It is one of the great star-forming nurseries in our part of the Milky Way.

The nebula holds enough gas to make 10,000 suns. It is mostly hydrogen, with helium, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen in decreasing amounts. At its heart sits the Trapezium, four extremely hot stars whose light makes the nebula shine. They are the brightest members of a sprawling cluster of several thousand young stars, many of them hidden inside the opaque gas and dust.

The Orion Nebula is easy to find with the unaided eye, yet there is apparently no written record of it before the 17th century. The image was made with the 1.5-metre Danish telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile.
explore: The picture combines three filters, with B for 60 seconds, V for 30 seconds and R for 21 seconds. East is at the upper right and north at the lower right. The nebula lies about 1,500 light-years away.

understand.summary: The Danish 1.54-metre telescope took this visible-light image through B, V and R filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The nebula is visible to the naked eye as a faint patch, but its colours and detail only appear in telescope exposures.

caption: The planetary nebula NGC 6781, imaged by the ESO 3.6-metre telescope
story: Shells of gas glow in intricate patterns around a faint central star in this picture of NGC 6781, a planetary nebula in the direction of the constellation Aquila, the Eagle.

Stars like our Sun lack the mass to end their lives as supernovae. Instead, before fading into dense, Earth-sized embers called white dwarfs, they cast off colourful shells of gas. These are known as planetary nebulae, a misleading name that comes from how these round clouds resembled giant planets through small telescopes.

Inside NGC 6781, shells of gas blown off the surface of the faint but very hot central star are expanding into space. Harsh ultraviolet light from the star makes them shine. Over time the star will steadily cool and darken until it disappears from view.
explore: The image was captured with EFOSC2, the ESO Faint Object Spectrograph and Camera, on the 3.6-metre telescope at La Silla Observatory in Chile. It used three wide-band filters and two narrow-band ones, and EFOSC2's field of view is 4.1 by 4.1 arcminutes.

understand.summary: The EFOSC2 instrument on the ESO 3.6-metre telescope took this visible-light image through B, V and R filters plus hydrogen-alpha and oxygen filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Narrow-band filters and long exposures reveal glowing shells too faint and too finely coloured for the eye.

scaleExtra: The nebula lies a few thousand light-years away and is approximately two light-years across, according to ESO.
